title: Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
Georgia caps refundable deposits (security, damage, pet and advance-rent deposits, but not nonrefundable fees or money to be applied to rent) at two months' rent for leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024.

The statute does not say when a month-to-month or other tenancy at will that began earlier counts as renewed, so apply the cap to every tenancy.

The statute does not say where an advance-rent deposit ends and prepaid rent begins, so treat last month's rent collected up front as a deposit, inside the cap and the escrow and return rules, unless the lease expressly makes it rent for a named calendar month.

A landlord must hold deposits in trust in an escrow account used only for deposits at a regulated bank or lending institution, and tell the tenant in writing where it is, or post a surety bond with the superior court clerk instead.

Before taking the deposit, the landlord must give the tenant a comprehensive list of existing damage to sign; within 3 business days after the lease ends and the tenant vacates (or surrenders and the landlord accepts), the landlord inspects and lists any damage charged against the deposit, with estimated costs, and the tenant may inspect within 5 business days. Both lists must tell the tenant of the duty to sign or dissent in writing.

Within 30 days after getting possession, the landlord returns the deposit or a written statement of the exact reasons for keeping any part, with the damage list and the balance, by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address; a returned, undeliverable refund becomes the landlord's 90 days after mailing if the tenant cannot be found.

Ordinary wear and tear cannot be charged. A landlord who misses the lists or the 30-day statement loses the right to withhold any part of the deposit and to sue for damage to the premises, and one who wrongfully keeps deposit money owes three times the amount plus attorney fees unless the error was a documented, unintentional bona fide mistake.

The escrow, bond, list and penalty sections do not apply to a natural person who, with spouse and minor children, owns ten or fewer rental units and does not pay a third party to manage them; the cap and the 30-day return still do. These rights cannot be waived in the lease.

title: Landlord's Repair and Fitness Duties
bodyText:
A Georgia landlord must keep the premises in repair and is liable for substantial improvements placed on the premises with the landlord's consent.

Every residential lease entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024 is deemed to include a promise that the premises is fit for human habitation; the statute does not say when a tenancy at will that began earlier counts as renewed, so treat the promise as part of every tenancy. Neither duty can be waived, assigned or avoided by the lease.

Georgia sets no statutory deadline for repairs and no statutory repair-and-deduct or rent-withholding procedure; the tenant's remedies come from the lease, contract law and the courts, and a tenant's good-faith repair request or code complaint is protected by the retaliation statute.

Once a landlord has parted with possession, it is not liable to third persons for the tenant's negligence or illegal use of the premises, but it is liable for damages from defective construction or from failing to keep the premises in repair.

Cities and counties may set minimum security standards to prevent unauthorized entry, and ordinances on unfit dwellings also apply and cannot be waived. A landlord may not knowingly and willfully cut off cooling, heat, light or water to a tenant before a dispossessory action is finally resolved. Air conditioning is not listed as a statutory repair item, but 'cooling' is a protected utility.

title: Lease Terms Georgia Law Voids
bodyText: In a Georgia residential lease, neither side may waive, assign, transfer or otherwise avoid the landlord's duty to keep the premises in repair and fit for habitation, the landlord's liability for failing to repair, local unfit-dwelling ordinances, the dispossessory (eviction) procedure, the distress-warrant procedure, the security-deposit rules, or applicable parts of the Civil Practice Act. A clause making the tenant pay the landlord's attorney fees when the tenant breaches is void unless the lease also makes the landlord pay the tenant's attorney fees when the landlord breaches. The servicemember termination right and the family-violence termination right cannot be waived or modified. A lease made for the purpose of prostitution is void. A blanket clause saying the landlord is not liable for the tenant's property or injuries cannot excuse the landlord's own failure to repair.

title: Dispossessory (Eviction) Notices and Process
bodyText: Georgia evictions are 'dispossessory' actions. For unpaid rent, late fees, utilities or other charges, the landlord first gives a written notice to vacate or pay all past-due amounts within three business days (for leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024; the statute does not say when a tenancy at will or month-to-month tenancy that began earlier counts as renewed, so give this notice for every tenancy); if the tenant neither pays nor leaves, the landlord files an affidavit with the magistrate or other court. For a holdover or a tenancy at will or at sufferance, the landlord first demands possession. Both the demand and the 3-day notice must be posted in a sealed envelope conspicuously on the door AND delivered by any additional method the lease specifies. The tenant is served and must answer within seven days; with no answer, the court issues a writ of possession immediately, but if service was made only by posting and mailing, no default money judgment can be entered unless the tenant answers or appears. In a nonpayment case the tenant can stop the case by tendering all rent claimed plus the warrant costs within seven days of service, but the landlord must accept that tender only once in any 12 months. If the case is not decided within two weeks, the tenant must pay rent into the court registry as it comes due. After judgment for the landlord, the writ takes effect seven days later unless the tenant appeals within seven days and pays rent into court. The officer removes the tenant and belongings, the landlord is not a bailee of them, and they are treated as abandoned once the writ is executed. The landlord must apply to execute the writ within 30 days. If the sheriff, constable or marshal cannot execute it within 14 days of the landlord's request, the landlord may use a certified off-duty officer, at the landlord's sole cost, but must give the sheriff, constable or marshal written notice of the date and time of the execution at least five calendar days in advance. A false statement in the affidavit or answer is a misdemeanor. If the property is a 'covered property' under the federal CARES Act, Georgia's magistrate court rules require the landlord to give the CARES Act 30-day notice to vacate before filing a nonpayment dispossessory, and the rules include a CARES Act affidavit form; which properties are covered is set by the federal statute. From January 1, 2027 a court may seal dispossessory records in the circumstances the statute lists.

title: Sealing Dispossessory Records
bodyText: From January 1, 2027, a Georgia court may, on motion and after a hearing, order the records of a dispossessory case made unavailable to the public when the tenant won the case; when the tenant has paid the judgment in full with interest and costs; or when seven years have passed since a dismissal or judgment, provided the judgment has been paid in full with interest and costs. Sealing does not stop the landlord from pursuing amounts owed in a separate action or through collections. Separately, and already in force, the Uniform Magistrate Court Rules (Rule 6(D)) and the Uniform Superior Court Rules (Rule 21) let any party ask the court to limit public access to a court file. The court may do so on finding that the harm to a person's privacy outweighs the public interest in access, and may enter a temporary order without notice for up to 30 days.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: A Georgia tenant makes a prima-facie case of retaliation by showing that, after the tenant in good faith exercised a legal or lease right, gave a notice to repair, complained to a code-enforcement agency or utility about a problem the landlord must fix, or organized or joined a tenant organization about habitability, the landlord within three months filed a dispossessory action, deprived the tenant of the premises without legal reason, cut services, raised the rent or ended the lease, or materially interfered with the tenant's lease rights. Retaliation is a defense to eviction, and the tenant may recover one month's rent plus $500, court costs, attorney fees if the conduct was willful, wanton or malicious, and declaratory relief, less any rent owed. It is not retaliation to raise rent or reduce services under a written escalation clause for utilities, taxes or insurance, as part of a building-wide pattern, or under a government program; or to evict or end a lease because rent was delinquent, because the tenant, family or a guest intentionally damaged property or threatened someone's safety, because the tenant breached written lease rules against serious misconduct or criminal acts, or because the tenant held over after either side's notice. A code inspection certifying compliance within the prior 12 months is a rebuttable defense.

title: Self-Help Eviction and Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Georgia's route to possession is the dispossessory action. It is a crime (fine up to $500) for a landlord knowingly and willfully to suspend cooling, heat, light or water service to a tenant until a dispossessory action against that tenant is finally resolved. If the tenant wins the dispossessory case, the landlord is liable for all foreseeable damages caused by its wrongful conduct. Georgia has no separate statute listing lockouts or removing doors as prohibited practices, and none sets a fixed money penalty for them; a landlord who takes possession outside the court process is exposed to tort claims under general law.

title: Ending a Tenancy With No Fixed Term
bodyText: Where no time is set for a Georgia tenancy to end, the law treats it as a tenancy at will. Ending a tenancy at will takes 60 days' notice from the landlord or 30 days' notice from the tenant. A tenant who stays after the term or after a proper notice is a tenant holding over, and the landlord demands possession and then files a dispossessory action. Georgia sets no separate week-to-week notice period and no rent-increase notice period.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: A Georgia servicemember (active duty in the regular or reserve armed forces or the Coast Guard, or Georgia National Guard on ordered federal duty of 90 days or more) may end a residential lease with written notice effective at least 30 days after the landlord receives it, with a copy of the orders or a commanding officer's verification, when the member gets permanent change of station orders to move 35 miles or more, is released from active duty and the unit is 35 miles or more from the home of record, is ordered into or becomes eligible for government quarters (on pain of losing housing allowance), gets temporary duty, change-of-station or state active duty orders over 60 days to an area 35 miles or more away, or gets a change of orders before moving in. The member owes only prorated rent to the termination date, and nothing at all if the notice comes 14 or more days before occupancy. An adult family member may terminate the same way if the member dies on active duty, with the orders or verification and the death certificate. These rights apply to leases entered on or after July 1, 2005 and cannot be waived. Separately, for a person on active duty who gets permanent change of station orders or temporary duty orders over three months, rent liability cannot exceed 30 days' rent after written notice and proof, plus repair of damage the tenant caused. Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) applies as well.

title: State Limits on Local Rent Regulation
bodyText: No Georgia county or city may enact, keep or enforce any ordinance or resolution that regulates in any way the amount of rent charged for privately owned single-family or multi-unit residential rental property. Local governments and their housing authorities may still regulate rents on property they own, and may enter agreements with private owners that regulate rent (for example, in exchange for public funding). Since July 1, 2025, a local government also may not require registration of residential rental property, and may inspect or investigate it only with probable cause to believe a code violation exists or has existed. Cities and counties may still set minimum security standards for rental dwellings and enforce unfit-dwelling ordinances, which a lease cannot waive. Other local ordinances are outside this library's scope.

title: Fair Housing
bodyText: The Georgia Fair Housing Act bars discrimination in renting because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin, the same classes as federal law; it adds no source-of-income, age or other class. It covers refusals to rent, different terms, discriminatory ads and statements, false unavailability, blockbusting, refusing reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (the landlord may require restoration where reasonable), refusing reasonable accommodations in rules and policies, and accessible design for multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991. A tenant whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety, or cause substantial physical damage to others' property, need not be accepted. Public housing may not restrict lawful firearm possession in a dwelling unless federal law requires it. Exempt, except for the advertising ban: a private owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a broker or discriminatory ads, and rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units. A court may impose civil penalties of up to $10,000, $25,000 or $50,000 for repeat violations, plus damages, punitive damages and fees; a private suit must be filed within two years.

title: Service Dogs: Georgia Penalties and Definitions
bodyText:
Since July 1, 2026, Georgia's service-dog law covers any person with a physical or mental impairment who is substantially limited in one or more activities of daily living over an extended period, and defines a service dog as a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks that directly assist that person and relate to the disability, or a dog in training under a trainer. A dog that only provides comfort, companionship or emotional support is not a service dog under Georgia law.

Such a person, or a trainer, has full and equal access to rental housing with a service dog and cannot be charged extra for it, but is liable for any damage the dog does; a landlord need not modify the property or give a higher degree of care.

Denying or interfering with these rights is a misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature, punishable by a fine of up to $2,000, up to 30 days in jail, or both. Deliberately misrepresenting oneself as qualified to use a service dog to get housing or other accommodations is the same grade of crime.

The rule does not reach a single-family home where no more than one room is rented. Emotional support animals are handled as reasonable accommodations under fair-housing law.

title: Out-of-State Owners Must Use a Georgia Broker
bodyText: Since July 1, 2025, a landlord who does not live in Georgia and owns or operates single-family or duplex rental property in Georgia must employ a real estate broker licensed in Georgia. If the broker lives outside Georgia, the broker must employ at least one person located in Georgia who is responsible for receiving, coordinating, managing and responding to tenants' communications about maintenance and other issues. The usual license exemptions for owners managing their own property and for full-time community-association employees do not apply to these non-resident landlords. If you own through an out-of-state LLC or corporation, it must get a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State before transacting business in Georgia, and until it does it cannot bring an eviction or other court case (its contracts stay valid and it can still defend a case); it also owes back fees and a penalty (O.C.G.A. §§ 14-11-702, 14-11-711, 14-2-1501, 14-2-1502). Owning property, without more, is not transacting business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts. If you rent under a name that does not show who owns the business, file a trade-name registration with the superior court clerk in the county where the business is mainly carried on and publish notice; failing to register is a misdemeanor and you will be charged court costs, but it does not defeat your lawsuit (O.C.G.A. §§ 10-1-490, 10-1-491, 10-1-493). Owning property in Georgia lets Georgia courts hear claims that arise from that ownership (O.C.G.A. § 9-10-91). Separately, since the same 2025 act, no Georgia city or county may require registration of residential rental property (see Code Inspections of Rental Property).

title: Lead Poisoning Hazards: Georgia Abatement Duties
bodyText:
Beyond the federal lead disclosure, Georgia's Lead Poisoning Prevention Act applies to owners and landlords who accept payment for residential rental property. When the Department of Public Health finds a lead poisoning hazard, it notifies the owner, the managing agent and the occupants.

When a child under six has a confirmed lead poisoning (3.5 micrograms per deciliter or more) and lives in or regularly visits the dwelling, the Department requires lead hazard abatement: the owner or managing agent must submit a written abatement plan within 30 days, give the Department and occupants three days' notice before work starts, and finish within 60 days of approval (extendable by 30 days); removing the children is not abatement if the unit stays in residential use. The Department can seek a court order.

An owner of pre-1978 housing who follows the statutory maintenance standard (repairing deteriorated paint, cleaning to the local customary standard at lease start, adjusting friction surfaces, cleaning carpets with the occupant's approval, keeping surfaces cleanable, and giving the federal lead information) every year and obtains an annual compliance certificate is shielded from liability for later injuries.

title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText: Georgia requires a listed smoke detector in every dwelling unit built on or after July 1, 1987, and at least a battery-operated smoke detector in good working order in every dwelling unit built before then. Detectors go on the ceiling or wall centrally in the corridor or area outside each group of sleeping rooms, and on every story including basements (split-level exception). The statute fines an OCCUPANT who fails to maintain a smoke detector in good working order up to $25, after a warning for the first violation; local building and fire officials may enforce it. A failure to maintain a detector is not evidence of negligence and cannot be used against anyone on liability or insurance. Georgia has no statute requiring carbon monoxide alarms in existing rental dwellings.

title: Bounced Checks
bodyText:
When a Georgia tenant's check, draft or order is dishonored for lack of funds or because there is no account, the landlord may charge a service charge of up to $30 or 5% of the face amount, whichever is greater, plus the bank's fees, when making written demand for payment.

If the tenant does not pay within 10 days after a written demand in the statutory form (sent by certified mail, statutory overnight delivery, or first-class mail supported by an affidavit of service), the landlord may sue in the county where the tenant lives for the check amount, the service charge and fees, plus damages of double the amount owed, capped at $500, and court costs. The court may waive the double damages for economic hardship. Paying in full before suit is a defense.

title: Towing Vehicles from Rental Property
bodyText:
A person entitled to possession of private property in Georgia may have a trespassing vehicle towed or booted only if a conspicuous notice is posted on the property saying unauthorized vehicles may be immobilized or removed at the owner's expense, with the full legal names of the company and the property owner, the boot-removal fee and contact, where the vehicle can be recovered, the cost and the forms of payment. Residential property with four or fewer units is exempt from the posting requirement.

Only towing and storage firms permitted by the local government or the Department of Public Safety may tow, and only Department-permitted operators in jurisdictions that authorize booting may boot. No storage fee may be charged for the first 24 hours.

A person injured by a violation may recover actual damages (presumed at least $100) and court costs, and three times actual damages for an intentional violation. A tow company may not pay a property owner for towing rights or patrol the lot for tows without a call for each case.

title: What a Landlord Need Not Disclose
bodyText: A Georgia owner or broker is not liable for failing to disclose that the property was occupied by someone with a disease medically shown to be highly unlikely to spread through occupancy, or that it was the site of a homicide, other felony, suicide, or accidental or natural death. But if asked, the owner or broker must answer truthfully to the best of their knowledge, unless answering would violate federal or state fair-housing or other law.

title: Removing Squatters and Intruders
bodyText: Georgia gives owners two routes against people who move in without permission. A person who enters and lives on another's property without the owner's knowledge or consent commits unlawful squatting, a misdemeanor; law enforcement issues a citation requiring the person to produce a lease, rental payment proof or other authorization within three business days, and if they cannot, they are subject to arrest. If they produce documents, a hearing is set within seven days, and invalid documents lead to removal, arrest and a fine based on market rent. Separately, an owner can swear an affidavit that a named person is in possession without a good-faith claim of right; an officer shows it to the occupant, who is removed after three days unless they file a counter-affidavit, which sends the matter to magistrate court for a non-jury trial, where the court may award fair market rent for the occupancy. These procedures are for intruders, not for tenants, who are removed only through a dispossessory action.

title: Undelivered and Uncashed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a Georgia landlord mails a deposit refund to the tenant's last known address by first-class mail and the letter comes back undelivered, and the landlord cannot find the tenant after reasonable effort, the refund becomes the landlord's property 90 days after it was mailed. A refund check that was delivered but never cashed is different: property held or owed in the ordinary course of business and unclaimed for more than five years is presumed abandoned under the unclaimed property act, with reporting and remittance duties to the state.

title: Rent Interest, Distress Warrants and the Landlord's Lien
bodyText: Unpaid rent in Georgia bears interest from the day it is due. When rent is due, or the tenant is trying to move property off the premises, a landlord may apply to a court for a distress warrant against the tenant's property; the tenant can answer, and tendering all rent plus costs within seven days of service is a complete defense. If the warrant is granted, the sheriff or marshal can levy on and sell the tenant's property. Two Georgia statutes date the landlord's lien differently: one says the landlord's lien for rent attaches when the landlord makes the distress-warrant affidavit and takes priority over no older lien except on crops raised on the premises; the other says the landlord's general lien on the tenant's property dates from the levy of a distress warrant and ranks behind tax liens and laborers' liens. Until a court settles which date governs, assume the later one, the levy, when judging the lien's priority against other creditors. A landlord may not seize the tenant's belongings without this court process. Destruction of the premises by fire or other casualty not caused by the landlord does not, by statute, reduce the rent; the lease can say otherwise, and Steinoak offers an optional clause that does.

title: Property Left Behind
bodyText: When a Georgia writ of possession is executed, the officer may remove the tenant and the tenant's belongings and place them on the landlord's property or another place the landlord designates and the officer approves; the landlord is not a bailee of the belongings, owes the tenant no duty for them, and after the writ is executed they are regarded as abandoned. A tenant's trade fixtures left after the term and possession end become the landlord's property. Georgia has no statute setting a notice, storage or sale procedure for belongings left after a tenant moves out voluntarily; the lease and general law govern.

title: No Late-Fee or Application-Fee Cap
bodyText: Georgia has no statute capping late fees or rental application fees for residential leases and no statutory grace period. Late fees are set by the lease. A lease late fee is liquidated damages, which binds the parties unless it violates some principle of law, so it should be a reasonable estimate of the landlord's loss. Unpaid late fees may be demanded in the 3-day notice to vacate or pay and kept from the security deposit.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: Georgia does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing account. The deposit must be held in trust in an escrow account (or covered by a surety bond) unless the small-landlord exemption applies.

title: No Statutory Entry-Notice Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute setting how much notice a landlord must give before entering a rented dwelling, the hours of entry, or the purposes for which a landlord may enter. Entry rights and notice come from the lease. A tenant's right to possession is otherwise protected by general law, and unreasonable interference within three months after protected tenant action can support a retaliation claim.

title: No Statutory Rent-Increase Notice
bodyText: Georgia sets no notice period for raising rent. During a fixed term the lease controls; a tenancy at will can be ended on 60 days' notice from the landlord, and a new rent is effectively offered through that process. Local rent control is preempted. A rent increase within three months after protected tenant action can support a retaliation claim unless it comes under a written escalation clause for utilities, taxes or insurance, is part of a building-wide pattern, or follows a government program's terms.

title: No Statewide Source-of-Income Rule
bodyText: Georgia's fair housing law does not protect source of income, and no Georgia statute requires a landlord to accept housing choice vouchers or other rental assistance. Some local ordinances may; they are outside this library's scope. Federal rules apply to landlords who choose to participate in the voucher program.

title: No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring or forbidding a landlord to ask about an applicant's or tenant's immigration status. National origin is a protected class under state and federal fair housing law, so status inquiries must not become a proxy for it.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring landlords to test for or disclose radon.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring landlords to disclose bed bugs, set a treatment timeline, or allocate treatment costs. Bed bugs fall under the landlord's general duty to keep the premises in repair and fit for human habitation, and the lease.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring landlords to disclose mold, set a treatment timeline, or allocate treatment costs. Mold falls under the landlord's general duty to keep the premises in repair and fit for human habitation, and the lease.

title: No Carbon Monoxide Alarm Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring carbon monoxide alarms in existing rental dwellings. Building codes adopted for new construction or renovation may require them.

title: No Drug-Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental was used as a methamphetamine or other drug lab, or setting a cleanup standard before re-renting.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving tenants a right to install electric-vehicle charging. The lease and the landlord's consent govern.

title: No Receipt Duty for Rent
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to give a receipt for rent, including cash rent. In a dispossessory case a tenant may show a receipt instead of paying disputed back rent into court, so receipts protect both sides.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Georgia has no general statute ending a residential lease when the tenant dies or setting a procedure for the tenant's belongings; the lease and estate law govern. The one exception is a servicemember who dies on active duty: an adult member of the immediate family may end the lease on 30 days' written notice with the orders or a commanding officer's verification and the death certificate.

title: No Statutory Holdover Damages
bodyText: Georgia sets no statutory measure of damages, such as double rent, for a tenant who holds over. The landlord recovers rent and other claims relating to the dispute in the dispossessory action, and any stipulated holdover rate in the lease is liquidated damages.

title: No Statutory Right-to-Call-Police Protection
bodyText: Georgia has no statute forbidding a lease from limiting a tenant's right to call the police or emergency services, or penalizing a tenant for doing so. Federal fair-housing law and local ordinances may still apply, and a lease term that penalizes calls for help by a domestic-violence victim carries fair-housing risk.

title: Family Violence or Stalking Order: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A tenant protected, with their minor child, by a civil or criminal family violence or stalking order may end the lease effective 30 days after giving you written notice with a copy of the order (and, for an ex parte temporary protective order, the police report), even as a joint tenant with no rent obligation (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-23). The tenant may stay until the termination takes effect and owes rent prorated to that date, payable when it would have been due, plus sums owed before termination, but no other fees, rent or damages for the early termination; if they end it 14 or more days before occupancy, nothing is owed. This right can't be waived or modified.

title: Flooding Notice Before Signing
bodyText: If flooding has damaged any part of the living space at least three times in the five years before the lease, give the prospective tenant a separate written flooding notice before the lease is signed (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-20). The lease's optional Flooding Notice clause carries the text and the tenant's acknowledgment.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and a tenancy with no end date (a tenancy at will, including month-to-month) ends on 60 days' notice from the landlord or 30 days' notice from the tenant, with no reason required; no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational. Within three months after a tenant in good faith exercises a legal or lease right, gives a notice to repair, complains to a code-enforcement agency or utility, or forms or joins a tenant organization about habitability, a landlord who files a dispossessory action, ends the lease or raises the rent faces a retaliation claim, unless the action rests on unpaid rent, intentional damage or threats, a breach of written lease rules against serious misconduct or criminal acts, or a holdover after notice ending the lease at the end of its term as the written lease provides. When an apartment building is converted to condominiums, the developer must give each qualifying tenant at least 120 days' notice and may not require the tenant to leave during that time except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants. Georgia has no repair rent-escrow procedure that bars eviction; the only rent paid into court is rent the tenant pays into the court registry while a dispossessory case is pending. Fair housing law applies.

title: Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText:
Georgia exempts from levy and sale a debtor's property worth up to $5,000, or up to $21,500 for property that is the debtor's primary residence. A debtor may waive that exemption in writing, including in the contract that creates the debt, except as to wearing apparel and $300 worth of household and kitchen furniture and provisions; after a levy the debtor can claim that $300 of property back by filing a schedule.

The library offers an optional waiver clause, off by default. Whether a residential lease counts as a 'contract of indebtedness' for this purpose, and how courts treat such waivers, is case law. It is a collection term aimed at the tenant that many residential leases leave out, so use it only as a deliberate choice.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText:
Georgia law leaves much of the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant.

Destruction by fire, or loss of possession through a casualty the landlord did not cause, does not reduce the rent unless the lease says otherwise, and the library's optional casualty clause gives no termination or rent reduction for damage caused by the tenant, household members, guests or invitees.

The landlord may keep from the security deposit the cost of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, including damage from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests, and may sue for the rest.

The landlord's statutory duty to keep the premises in repair has no stated exception for damage the tenant caused and cannot be waived; whether courts relieve a landlord of it in that case is case law.

No Georgia statute measures the landlord's lost rent if the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage; the library offers an optional clause that does.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Georgia law makes rent bear interest from the time it is due. Where the lease states no rate, the legal rate is 7% a year simple interest. Parties may set a different rate by written contract, but where the principal amount involved is $3,000 or less, the rate on a forbearance to enforce the collection of a sum of money may not exceed 16% a year simple interest, and Georgia defines interest broadly, as a charge for the use of money computed in any way or form. The library offers no interest clause. A landlord who wants a contract rate can add one, and should take advice first.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Georgia statutes do not regulate the use of algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents. Georgia also has no rent control and bars cities and counties from regulating the amount of rent on private rental property ("State Limits on Local Rent Regulation"). Federal antitrust law may still apply.

title: Fees and the Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText:
Georgia's eviction statute names fees alongside rent rather than treating them as rent. For leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024, when a tenant fails to pay the rent, late fees, utilities or other charges owed to the landlord, the landlord may give a notice to vacate or pay all of them within three business days and then file a dispossessory action.

Other steps still turn on rent: a tenant can stop a nonpayment case by tendering all rents claimed plus the cost of the dispossessory warrant within seven days of service (the landlord must accept that only once in any 12 months), and while a case is pending the tenant pays into the court registry the rent and utility payments the lease makes the tenant's responsibility.

The library's shared Default clause gives up one part of this on purpose: except where the law requires otherwise, an unpaid late fee alone, apart from the Rent itself, does not let the landlord end the lease or evict. Other unpaid charges are not covered by that sentence.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant failed to do, and add the cost to the rent. No provision of Georgia's landlord-tenant chapter gives a landlord that right, sets a notice period for it, or makes the cost rent. What Georgia law does give: the landlord may keep from the security deposit the cost of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, may sue for the rest, and for unpaid charges owed to the landlord may use the three-business-day notice to vacate or pay. Whether a repair cost the lease makes the tenant's responsibility is such a charge is not settled by the statute's text.

title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText:
Georgia imposes no statutory requirement that a written residential lease have every blank completed, and none that the landlord give the tenant a signed copy. Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act reaches residential leases, but its list of unlawful practices has no blank-space or copy-at-signing item for an ordinary lease.

Several Georgia rules still turn on what the lease says: the owner and agent disclosure, the statement of where the deposit is held, and any delivery methods for the three-day notice and demand for possession that the lease adds to posting on the door. A blank left in one of those is a right or a duty left unclear.

Fill in every blank before signing and give the tenant a copy, as good practice rather than a statutory duty.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Georgia's statutes contain no covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession running from the landlord to the tenant. Possession is protected instead by the dispossessory process: a landlord recovers possession through a court action and a writ executed by an officer, not by self-help ("Self-Help Eviction and Utility Shutoffs"). Whether Georgia implies a covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease is case law; case notes in the official code refer to one.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Georgia prescribes no form for a residential lease, and none for the three-day notice to vacate or pay or the demand for possession; the statute prescribes how those notices are delivered (posted in a sealed envelope on the door, plus any method the lease adds), not their wording. Two prescribed forms can reach a landlord: the written demand sent before suing on a dishonored check, which must be in substantially the statutory form ("Bounced Checks"), and, for a property covered by the federal CARES Act, the CARES Act affidavit form in the Uniform Magistrate Court Rules ("Dispossessory (Eviction) Notices and Process").

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Georgia statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras, video doorbells or similar devices. The lease's alteration terms govern; in this library that is the Alterations section, which requires the landlord's written consent before a tenant adds or changes a fixture. Georgia's eavesdropping and surveillance laws, and any homeowners' association rules, may limit what a camera records rather than its installation.

title: Security Deposit Cap
bodyText:
Georgia caps a security deposit at the equivalent of two months' rent: you may not demand or receive more. Add every refundable deposit together before you check the cap, because damage deposits, advance-rent deposits and pet deposits are all security deposits.

Nonrefundable fees, and money that is to be applied to rent or to pay for services or utilities you provide, are not deposits and do not count toward it.

The cap came in with the 2024 Safe at Home Act, which applies to leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024. The act does not say when an older month-to-month tenancy counts as renewed, so apply the cap to every tenancy. The exemption for an owner of ten or fewer units does not reach the cap. See Security Deposit Rules for the escrow, damage-list and return duties.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Georgia residential lease cannot waive, assign, transfer or otherwise avoid any right, duty or remedy in the security deposit article: the two-month cap, the escrow account or bond, the move-in and move-out damage lists, the 30-day return and written statement, and the tenant's remedies for a wrongful withholding. The bar runs both ways, so the article's protections for you, such as the tenant's duty to sign or dissent from a damage list, cannot be bargained away either. Do not rely on a lease term that shortens, conditions or trims these rules; write deposit terms that repeat or add to the statute. For a natural person who, with spouse and minor children, owns ten or fewer rental units and does not pay a third party to manage them, the escrow, bond, damage-list and penalty sections do not apply at all, but the cap and the 30-day return still do.

title: Losing the Right to Keep a Deposit
bodyText: Georgia has three deposit penalties. First, the statute bars you from keeping any part of the deposit if you did not escrow it or post a bond, did not give the tenant the move-in damage list, and did not compile the move-out list on time. The statute joins those three failures with "and", so read literally all three must fail; a court may read it more broadly, so treat any one of them as fatal. Second, if you do not provide the damage lists and the written statement within the 30-day return period, you forfeit every right to withhold any of the deposit and to sue the tenant for damage to the premises. Third, if you fail to return deposit money you were required to return, you owe the tenant three times the amount wrongly withheld plus reasonable attorney fees, unless you prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the withholding was unintentional and came from a bona fide error despite procedures reasonably designed to avoid it; then you owe only the amount withheld. None of the three penalties applies to a natural person who, with spouse and minor children, owns ten or fewer rental units and does not pay a third party to manage them, because the exemption reaches the whole penalty section. A tenant who was at the move-out inspection and either signed the list or did not dissent in writing cannot recover the deposit or these damages, but only if both lists carried written notice of the duty to sign or dissent.

title: Last Month's Rent Collected Up Front
bodyText: Georgia's deposit definition includes "advance rent deposits" but leaves out money that is to be applied toward rent. The statute does not say where one ends and the other begins. The cautious course is to treat last month's rent collected at signing as a deposit, counted toward the two-month cap and held and returned under the deposit rules, unless the lease expressly makes it rent for a named calendar month. No Georgia statute lets a tenant apply the deposit to the last month's rent or forbids it. If the tenant does not pay the last month, you may keep deposit money for the unpaid rent, listed in your written statement within 30 days after you get possession.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText:
Georgia does not cap pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent separately. A refundable pet deposit is a security deposit: it counts toward the two-month cap and is held, listed and returned under the deposit rules.

A pet fee that you and the tenant agree in the lease will not be refunded is a nonrefundable fee, outside the deposit rules and the cap; use the lease's Nonrefundable Fees terms to say so. You may keep deposit money for unpaid pet fees. Monthly pet rent is rent in this library's reading.

For an assistance animal, see Service Dogs and Other Assistance Animals before charging any pet deposit, fee or rent.

title: No Separate Notice of a Nonrefundable Fee
bodyText: Georgia does not require a separate written notice, at the time you collect money, that part of it is nonrefundable. What makes a fee nonrefundable is the lease itself: the statute defines a nonrefundable fee as money paid under the rental agreement that the parties agreed would not be refunded. So state each nonrefundable fee and its amount in the lease (the library's Nonrefundable Fees clause does this). Money you hold as security without that agreement is a security deposit, inside the two-month cap and the return rules.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, and it has no rule on charging different tenants different deposits. The only statutory limit on the amount is the two-month cap. Fair housing law still governs how you set deposits, so apply the same standards to every applicant.

title: No Deposit Instalment Right
bodyText: No Georgia statute gives a tenant the right to pay the security deposit in instalments, and none requires you to offer one; you may ask for the whole deposit before occupancy. If you agree to instalments, write the amounts and dates into the lease. Each instalment is still security deposit money: it counts toward the two-month cap, goes into the escrow account (or is covered by your bond) unless you are a small owner exempt from those rules, and is returned under the deposit rules. Unless you are a small owner exempt from the damage-list rules, the move-in damage list must be given to the tenant before the deposit is tendered, so give it before the first instalment.

title: Deposit Return Does Not Depend on Move-Out Notice
bodyText: Georgia does not make the deposit refund depend on the tenant's notice of move-out or a forwarding address. The 30-day clock runs from when you obtain possession. If the tenant leaves or surrenders without telling you, you must (unless you are a small owner exempt from the damage-list rules) inspect and make the move-out damage list within a reasonable time after you discover the vacancy, sign it, and then return the deposit or your written statement within the 30 days. You satisfy the return duty by mailing the statement and any refund first class to the tenant's last known address; if it comes back undelivered and you cannot find the tenant after reasonable effort, the money becomes yours 90 days after mailing. You may ask for a forwarding address in the lease, but do not make the refund conditional on it, because the deposit rules cannot be waived.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Georgia has no expedited procedure for a deposit after an eviction or abandonment, and no statute authorizes a processing or administrative fee for handling it. The ordinary rules apply: unless you are a small owner exempt from the damage-list rules, inspect and list damage within three business days after the lease ends and you get possession (or within a reasonable time after you discover an unannounced vacancy), then return the deposit or your written statement within 30 days. You may keep deposit money for unpaid rent and late fees, abandonment of the premises, unpaid utilities, cleaning or repairs the tenant contracted for with third parties, unpaid pet fees, and actual damages from the tenant's breach, provided you try to mitigate. If a court finds neither side entitled to some of the deposit, it orders an equitable division.

title: Holding Deposits Taken Before the Lease
bodyText: Georgia has no statute written for holding deposits, reservation fees or other money taken from an applicant before a lease is signed. The deposit article reaches money held "by virtue of a residential rental agreement", so it does not clearly cover money taken before any agreement exists. The cautious course: if you take a holding deposit, give the applicant a signed writing that states the amount, what it holds, when it will be refunded and when you may keep it. Once a lease is signed, apply the money to the deposit or rent and count any part kept as security toward the two-month cap. A real estate broker who accepts the money must deposit it in the broker's trust or escrow account.

title: Fees in Lieu of a Deposit
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on deposit-alternative programs, such as a monthly fee or insurance product offered instead of a security deposit. Such a fee is lawful only as an ordinary contract term. If the payment is nonrefundable and the lease says so, it is a nonrefundable fee outside the deposit rules and the two-month cap; if any of it is held as security for the tenant's performance, it is a security deposit, whatever it is called, and the cap, escrow and return rules apply. Do not require a tenant to take the alternative, and tell the tenant in writing whether the fee is refundable and what it does and does not cover. The only statutory alternative in Georgia is yours: a surety bond filed with the superior court clerk instead of an escrow account.

title: Application Fees
bodyText: Georgia does not cap rental application or screening fees, require a refund when you turn an applicant down or rent to someone else, or regulate when you may cash the fee. An application fee is usually paid before any lease exists, so state in the signed application what it covers and whether it is refundable. If any part is held as security and a lease follows, that part is a security deposit. Screening itself is governed by federal law (consumer reports, fair housing).

title: Utility Deposits You Hold
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on a separate utility deposit held by a landlord. If you collect money to secure the tenant's utility bills, treat it as part of the security deposit: it is security held for the tenant, so it counts toward the two-month cap and is held and returned under the deposit rules, and you may keep it for unpaid utility charges. Money that is to be applied to utilities you provide is not a deposit. Deposits a utility company takes from its own customer are the utility's, under its own rules.

title: No All-In Rent or Fee Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no rental fee-transparency or all-in pricing law: no rule that advertised or lease rent include every mandatory fee, and no required first-page fee disclosure. Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act reaches residential leases and bars unfair or deceptive acts in consumer transactions, so a fee hidden from the applicant or added without basis in the lease is a risk under that act. State every fee and its amount in the lease.

title: No Required List of Fees in the Lease
bodyText: Georgia does not require a residential lease to list every fee and charge, or set a notice period before you add one. Treat the lease as the source of every fee: collect only fees it provides for, and get the tenant's written agreement before adding one mid-term. A fee the lease provides for can be included in the three-business-day notice to vacate or pay with past-due rent, so list each fee, its amount and when it is due.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Georgia has no statute written to bar a fee for a service you do not provide. A charge with nothing behind it is still a risk: the Fair Business Practices Act bars unfair or deceptive acts in consumer transactions, including residential leases. Make sure every fee in the lease matches something you actually provide or a cost you actually incur.

title: No Separate Late-Fee Limit for Mobile Home Parks
bodyText: Georgia has no late-fee cap for any residential tenancy, and no separate cap for mobile home park tenants or for utility charges. A late fee is set by the lease. Agreed damages bind unless they violate some principle of law, and whether a late fee is a penalty is for the courts, so set it as a reasonable estimate of your loss from late payment. See No Late-Fee or Application-Fee Cap.

title: Attorney Fees in a Georgia Lease
bodyText: A Georgia residential lease term making the tenant pay your attorney fees when the tenant breaches is void unless the same term also makes you pay the tenant's attorney fees when you breach. The library's default clause uses a mutual prevailing-party sentence for that reason. Without a valid fee term, each side pays its own lawyer, except that, when the plaintiff has pleaded for them, the jury may allow litigation expenses against a defendant who acted in bad faith, was stubbornly litigious or caused unnecessary trouble and expense, and except that a tenant who recovers a wrongfully withheld deposit gets three times the amount plus reasonable attorney fees by statute, unless the landlord proves a bona fide error or is a small owner exempt from that penalty. Georgia's separate statute on attorney fees in notes and other evidence of indebtedness caps a percentage fee at 15 percent and requires a ten-day written notice before the fee can be enforced; whether it reaches a lease is a question of case law, so if you rely on a lease fee term to collect unpaid rent, also send that ten-day notice.

title: Agreed Damages in a Georgia Lease
bodyText:
Georgia enforces damages the parties fix in their contract, such as a late fee, an early termination fee or a daily holdover charge, unless the agreement "violates some principle of law". The statute gives no further test. Whether a fixed amount is enforceable or is a penalty is decided by the courts.

The cautious course is to set each agreed amount as a reasonable estimate of a loss that is hard to measure in advance, keep it in proportion to the rent, and avoid amounts that grow with the length of the remaining term.

Deposit deductions follow their own list: you may keep deposit money for unpaid rent and late fees, abandonment, unpaid utilities, cleaning or repairs the tenant contracted for, unpaid pet fees, and actual damages from the tenant's breach if you try to mitigate them, but never for ordinary wear and tear.

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Georgia has no statute that allows or bars a collection fee on past-due rent as such. A fee to cover collection costs is an agreed-damages term: it can bind only if the lease provides for it, and whether it is a penalty is for the courts, so keep it to a reasonable estimate of your actual cost. A term making the tenant pay your attorney fees for collection is void unless it is mutual. If a collection agency collects for you, the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bars it from collecting any amount that the lease does not expressly authorize and the law does not permit. Unpaid rent also bears interest from the day it is due.

title: Fees for Serving Notices or Filing
bodyText: Georgia has no statute that allows or bars a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice, such as the three-day notice to vacate or pay, or for filing a dispossessory. Such a charge is an agreed-damages term; whether it binds or is a penalty is for the courts, so keep it to a reasonable estimate of your actual cost. Court costs are different: the court awards them in the case, and a tenant who stops a nonpayment case by tender must pay the cost of the dispossessory warrant. A lease term making the tenant pay your attorney fees is void unless it is mutual.

title: No Statutory Ban on Eviction Charges
bodyText: Georgia has no statute that bans a lease clause charging the tenant for an eviction. The limits come from general law: an agreed charge is enforceable only as agreed damages, and whether it is a penalty is for the courts, so keep it a reasonable estimate of loss; a one-way attorney-fee term is void; and the dispossessory procedure itself cannot be waived or avoided by the lease. Keep any such charge tied to your documented actual cost.

title: Time Limits for Suing a Tenant
bodyText: In Georgia, a suit on a written lease for unpaid rent or other money must be brought within six years after the amount became due and payable; if the lease recites in its body that it is under seal, the period is 20 years after the right of action accrues. A suit on an oral lease, an implied promise or an open account must be brought within four years after the right of action accrues. A new promise to pay restarts the period only if it is in writing, in the tenant's own handwriting or signed by the tenant or someone the tenant authorized; a payment the tenant notes on a written record of the debt, or another written acknowledgment of the debt, counts as such a promise. Do not rely on an unwritten payment or promise to extend your time.

title: Arbitration Clauses in a Georgia Residential Lease
bodyText:
Georgia's arbitration code does not apply to contracts involving consumer transactions, and a residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Fair Business Practices Act. That takes the lease out of the state arbitration code; it does not make an arbitration clause unlawful, and no Georgia statute penalizes including one.

Federal law fills the gap: the Federal Arbitration Act makes a written arbitration agreement in a contract involving interstate commerce enforceable, applies in state courts, and has been held to reach the rental of real estate.

On that basis the library offers an optional clause: money claims only, with possession (the dispossessory procedure, which the lease cannot waive), small claims, security-deposit, injury, emergency and government-agency matters kept out, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials.

A court here could still refuse to enforce it; if one did, the dispute would simply go to court.

title: No Preset Cleaning or Damage Charges
bodyText: Georgia has no statute that lets a lease preset cleaning or damage charges against the deposit, and none that prescribes a notice for doing so. What the deposit statute does is limit what you may keep: you may not keep any part of the deposit for ordinary wear and tear, and, unless you are a small owner exempt from the list rules, a damage deduction must rest on the move-out damage list with the estimated dollar value of each item. So a flat cleaning or carpet charge cannot stand in for that list. You may keep the deposit for cleaning or repair work the tenant itself contracted for with a third party and left unpaid, and for actual damages caused by the tenant's breach of the lease, provided you try to mitigate them.

title: Security Deposits When You Sell
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on what happens to tenants' deposits when the property is sold or transferred, and none that makes a buyer liable for deposits the seller collected or releases the seller once deposits are handed over. While you hold a deposit it is held in trust for the tenant in an escrow account (unless you are an exempt owner of ten or fewer units or have posted the surety bond, which also covers foreclosure and your bankruptcy). The safe course on a sale is to transfer each deposit to the buyer, have the buyer agree in writing to hold and return it under the deposit statute, and tell the tenant in writing where the deposit is now held. The new owner or manager must also be disclosed to the tenant within 30 days of the change.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on carpet cleaning: nothing lets you require professional cleaning at move-out as a matter of law, and nothing bars a lease term requiring it. Two limits apply. You may not keep any deposit money for ordinary wear and tear, so a deduction is safest when the carpets were professionally cleaned before the tenancy and the move-in damage list records their condition. And a deduction is for actual damages caused by the tenant's breach: charge only the reasonable cost you actually pay, and list it on the move-out damage list with its dollar value (unless you are a small owner exempt from the list rules, in which case state it in the written statement). There is no age or depreciation formula for carpet or paint. If the tenant hired a cleaner and left the bill unpaid, you may keep that amount.

title: Georgia's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Georgia sets few money limits on a residential lease. Security deposit: no more than two months' rent; the act reaches leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024, and the library applies the cap to every tenancy. Bounced check: a service charge of up to $30 or 5% of the face amount, whichever is greater, plus bank fees, and after a 10-day written demand, damages of double the amount owed up to $500. Interest on unpaid rent runs from the due date, at 7% a year simple interest unless the lease sets a rate (on $3,000 or less, keep any lease rate at or below 16% a year). There is no cap on late fees, application fees, pet fees or other nonrefundable fees, and no rent control; agreed charges bind unless they violate some principle of law; the safe course is to keep them reasonable estimates of loss. Attorney-fee terms must be mutual.

title: Selling or Changing Managers
bodyText: When the owner of record, the service agent or the manager changes, for example on a sale or when you hire a manager, you must tell each tenant the new names and addresses within 30 days, in writing or by a notice posted in a conspicuous place. Georgia has no statute releasing a selling landlord from the lease or the deposit, none making a buyer liable for the seller's deposits, and no seller-disclosure or estoppel-certificate rule tied to a rented dwelling, so handle the deposits by contract in the sale (see Security Deposits When You Sell). A person who signs leases for you without making the owner and manager disclosure becomes your agent for service and for your duties, and must make the rent collected available to meet them.

title: When a Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText:
Georgia has no landlord-tenant statute on what a tenant owes after abandoning the home, and none that sets a duty to re-rent.

Two statutes bear on it. A party injured by a breach of contract must lessen the damages as far as is practicable with ordinary care and diligence; whether and how that applies to rent for the rest of a lease term is for the courts. And you may keep deposit money for abandonment of the premises, and for actual damages from the breach provided you attempt to mitigate those damages.

The cautious course: after an abandonment, make documented efforts to re-rent at a fair rent, credit what you receive, and claim only the loss that remains.

title: Agreeing on Extra Ways to Deliver Notices
bodyText: Georgia lets the lease add delivery methods for the two notices that start a dispossessory: the demand for possession and the three-business-day notice to vacate or pay. Each must be posted in a sealed envelope conspicuously on the door of the property and also delivered by any additional method agreed in the rental agreement, for example e-mail or text message. So if the lease names extra methods, use every one of them as well as posting; leaving one out risks the notice. Georgia has no general "actual notice" rule for other landlord-tenant notices.

title: No Confession of Judgment in a Lease
bodyText: Do not put a confession-of-judgment or warrant-of-attorney clause in a Georgia residential lease. Georgia lets a party confess judgment only in an action already filed and docketed, in the county where the defendant lived when the action began; nothing allows a judgment entered in advance on the strength of a lease clause. And a residential lease cannot waive or avoid the dispossessory procedure, under which the tenant is served and may answer with any legal or equitable defense or counterclaim.

title: Eviction Grounds and Cure Rights
bodyText:
A Georgia dispossessory lies when a tenant holds over beyond the term, when a tenant at will or at sufferance stays after the tenancy ends, and when a tenant fails to pay rent, late fees, utilities or other charges. For nonpayment you must first give a notice to vacate or pay within three business days.

For other breaches the statute sets no notice period and no right to cure; the lease decides whether a breach ends the tenancy, and then you demand possession. The statute does not say which breaches are serious enough, so give a written notice describing the breach and a reasonable time to cure before ending the lease for anything short of a serious breach.

A tenant who tenders all rent claimed plus the warrant cost within seven days of service ends a nonpayment case; you must accept that once in any 12 months.

title: No Hardship Stay of Eviction
bodyText: Georgia has no statute letting a court delay an eviction for the tenant's hardship. After judgment for the landlord the writ of possession takes effect seven days after judgment, and an appeal filed within those seven days keeps the tenant in possession only while the tenant pays the rent found due and future rent into court. The landlord must apply to execute the writ within 30 days of its issue, or show good cause for the delay, or apply for a new writ.

title: No Expedited Eviction for Criminal Activity
bodyText: Georgia has no faster eviction track for drug activity, violent crime or other criminal conduct. An eviction for criminal activity proceeds like any other dispossessory: end the tenancy under the lease, demand possession, and file. The tenant has seven days to answer, and the case is tried if the tenant answers. The 2024 Safe at Home Act did not add an expedited track.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Case
bodyText: In a Georgia nonpayment dispossessory the tenant may, within seven days after being served, tender all rent claimed plus the cost of the dispossessory warrant. That tender is a complete defense, and you must accept it, but only once in any 12-month period for the same tenant. If you refuse a tender you were required to take, the court orders the tenant to pay within three days, and a writ issues if the tenant does not. Georgia has no forfeiture-election rule for the notice and no redemption right after judgment.

title: Redeeming the Tenancy
bodyText: A Georgia tenant sued for nonpayment can save the tenancy by tendering all rent claimed plus the dispossessory warrant cost within seven days after service; you must accept that once in any 12 months. Georgia has no statute requiring reservation wording when you accept partial rent, no redemption right after judgment, and no rule on payment by a charity or agency. The statute says only that, for a non-residential tenant, accepting less than all rent claimed is not a bar or defense; it is silent for residential tenants, and whether accepting part payment waives the case is for the courts. So if you accept part payment and still want possession, say so in writing when you accept it.

title: No Good-Cause or Protected-Tenant Notice
bodyText: Georgia has no good-cause eviction rule, so it has no good-cause notice and no required notice of special protections for older, disabled or long-term tenants. A tenancy at will ends on 60 days' notice from you or 30 days' from the tenant, and a fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term. Retaliation is still barred, and federal programs and some subsidized housing have their own cause and notice rules.

title: Possession and Money After the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: A Georgia dispossessory recovers both possession and money: if you win, judgment is entered for all rents due and for any other claim relating to the dispute, with a writ of possession. But if the tenant was served only by posting and mailing and does not answer, you get possession by default and no money judgment. Rent and damages can also be sued for separately, within the limitation periods. Georgia also keeps the distress warrant for rent and the landlord's lien. You cannot take possession yourself; the dispossessory is the remedy.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Georgia gives no self-help lockout for unpaid rent, and a lease cannot create one. The dispossessory procedure is the only way to recover possession, and a residential lease cannot waive or avoid it. Knowingly and willfully cutting off cooling, heat, light or water before the dispossessory is finally decided is a crime with a fine of up to $500. Do not change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or shut off utilities to press for rent.

title: The Three-Day Notice to Vacate or Pay
bodyText: Before filing for nonpayment you must give the tenant a notice to vacate or pay all past due rent, late fees, utilities and other charges within three business days. Post it in a sealed envelope conspicuously on the door and also deliver it by every additional method the lease names. Georgia prescribes no wording, so the notice should state the amount due by category, the three-business-day deadline and that you will file if the tenant neither pays nor leaves. A public housing authority may give it with the federal termination notice, in a separate writing. The notice is a separate writing given after the rent is late, so the lease itself cannot serve as it, and the tenant's tender defense is limited to once in 12 months.

title: Eviction Notices Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Georgia residential lease cannot shorten or waive the demand for possession, the three-business-day notice to vacate or pay, or any other part of the dispossessory procedure; do not rely on a clause that tries. The 60-day and 30-day notices that end a tenancy at will are set by statute, and the library treats them as fixed too.

title: While a Notice or Eviction Is Pending
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on alterations or other conduct while a notice to vacate is pending. One rule does apply: you may not knowingly and willfully cut off cooling, heat, light or water until the dispossessory is finally decided. Your duty to keep the premises in repair continues until the tenant leaves.

title: Rent Into Court Instead of a Possession Bond
bodyText: Georgia has no possession bond. Instead, if the right to possession is not decided within two weeks after service, the tenant must pay rent and utility payments into the court registry as they come due, plus the amount claimed before the warrant (or a receipt showing it was paid), and a writ issues on any missed payment. On appeal the tenant stays only by paying the rent found due and future rent into court.

title: Belongings Removed Under a Writ
bodyText: A Georgia writ of possession authorizes removing the tenant and the tenant's belongings and placing them on part of your property or other property you designate and the executing officer approves. You are not a bailee of those belongings and owe the tenant no duty for them, and after the writ is executed they are treated as abandoned. Georgia has no storage, inventory or notice duty after a writ and no rule on pets left behind; for animals, contact local animal control rather than leaving them. If the tenant does not move a mobile home or other transportable housing within ten days after the final order, you may have it moved at the tenant's expense by a licensed carrier, who has a lien for moving and storage fees. Staying after notice to depart, or entering after notice that entry is forbidden, is criminal trespass.

title: No Statutory Bar on Demanding Rent for an Unfit Unit
bodyText: Georgia has no statute barring you from demanding or collecting rent, or serving a notice to vacate or pay, while the home is unfit. But every residential lease includes a promise that the premises are fit for human habitation, and you must keep them in repair, duties the lease cannot waive. A tenant may raise your breach as a defense or counterclaim in the dispossessory, so fix serious defects before pressing for rent.

title: Tenant Answers, Counterclaims and Rent Into Court
bodyText: A Georgia tenant answers a dispossessory orally or in writing within seven days after service and may raise any legal or equitable defense or counterclaim. A tenant who answers stays in possession pending the outcome but must pay rent into the court registry, and if possession is not decided within two weeks of service the tenant pays rent and utility payments as they come due plus the amount claimed before the warrant; a missed payment means a writ issues. The court pays you the undisputed funds as they come in.

title: The Repair Duty Cannot Be Assigned Away
bodyText: In a Georgia residential lease you may not waive, assign, transfer or otherwise avoid your duty to keep the premises in repair or your liability for failing to repair, by the lease or any similar agreement. Georgia has no statute that separates the right to collect rent from the repair duty, but the non-waiver rule means whoever is the landlord keeps the repair duty while collecting rent.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: Georgia law gives you one way to remove a tenant: the dispossessory, which a residential lease cannot waive. Do not change the locks, remove the tenant's belongings or cut off utilities to force a tenant out. Knowingly and willfully suspending cooling, heat, light or water before the dispossessory is finally decided is a crime, with a fine of up to $500. If a dispossessory ends in judgment for the tenant, you are liable for all foreseeable damages your wrongful conduct caused. Damages for a self-help eviction outside a dispossessory come from case law.

title: No Late-Benefit Defense
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving a tenant a continuance or defense when rent is late because a Social Security, voucher or other government payment is late. The tender defense still applies: payment of all rent claimed plus the warrant cost within seven days of service ends the case; you must accept that once in any 12 months. Federal program rules may add notice or other duties for subsidized tenancies.

title: When a Tenant Files Bankruptcy
bodyText: Georgia law has no rule on enforcing a writ after a tenant files bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law controls. The automatic stay stops a dispossessory, but it does not stop an eviction where you got a judgment for possession before the petition, subject to a limited cure procedure that depends on state law letting the tenant cure after judgment (Georgia's statute provides none after judgment), or an eviction based on endangering the property or illegal drug use, if you file and serve the required certification. Get bankruptcy counsel before acting after a filing.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice or Breach
bodyText: No Georgia statute decides whether accepting rent after a demand for possession, a notice to vacate or pay, or with knowledge of a breach waives the notice or the breach; that is case law. The cautious course: once you have demanded possession or decided to end the tenancy, refuse or return further rent, or accept it only with a written statement that acceptance does not waive the notice, the breach or your right to possession. Accepting a full tender within seven days of service ends a nonpayment case by statute.

title: What a Tenant Can Recover When You Breach
bodyText: Georgia gives tenants few statutory remedies of their own. Your repair and fitness duties, and your liability for failing to repair, cannot be waived. A tenant may raise your breach as a defense or counterclaim in a dispossessory, and if the tenant wins you are liable for all foreseeable damages your wrongful conduct caused. Deposit violations carry their own penalties, and retaliation gives the tenant statutory remedies. Repair-and-deduct and rent withholding are not in the statutes; they come from case law.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: When no end date is set for a Georgia tenancy, the law treats it as a tenancy at will. It ends on 60 days' notice from you or 30 days' notice from the tenant. A tenant at will who stays after the tenancy ends, or a tenant at sufferance, can be removed by dispossessory after a demand for possession. Whether a written month-to-month lease is a tenancy at will for these notice periods is for the courts; the cautious course is to give 60 days' notice yourself and accept 30 days' from the tenant unless the lease gives longer. Oral leases of up to one year are valid.

title: When the Law Lets a Tenant End the Lease Early
bodyText:
Georgia lets a tenant end a residential lease early in two situations: a service member who receives qualifying military orders, and a tenant protected by a family violence or stalking order. A service member's rent liability after written notice and proof of orders is also capped at 30 days' rent plus damage repair.

Georgia's landlord-tenant statutes give no early termination right for a landlord's misrepresentation; under general contract law a party defrauded may rescind, but only by promptly restoring, or offering to restore, anything of value received under the lease, so get advice before treating a misrepresentation as ending the lease.

A fire or other casualty not caused by you or by a defect in your title does not by statute end the lease or abate the rent; the lease decides that.

title: No Cold-Weather or Holiday Eviction Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute barring or delaying evictions in cold weather, extreme heat or on holidays, and no extra notice before vacating in winter. The writ takes effect seven days after judgment and must be applied for within 30 days. Utilities may not be cut off before the dispossessory is finally decided. Some sheriffs and marshals set their own scheduling practices; check locally.

title: No Termination for Illness or Incapacity
bodyText: Georgia has no statute letting a tenant end a lease because of illness, disability, incapacity or a move to care, and none ending a tenancy at will on a party's incapacity. A tenant at will keeps the right to crops planted before you gave notice ending the tenancy, or when the tenancy ends suddenly, such as on a party's death. A lessee of someone who held only a life estate has limited rights when that estate ends. Disability accommodation requests are a fair-housing matter.

title: Barring Trespassers From the Property
bodyText: Under Georgia's criminal trespass statute, a person who knowingly and without authority enters your land or premises after the owner, the rightful occupant or an authorized representative has told them entry is forbidden, or who stays after being told to leave, commits a misdemeanor. A tenant is a rightful occupant of the unit, so a trespass warning should be limited to common areas you control and should not bar the tenant's own guests from reaching the unit without a lease basis. Give the notice in writing and keep a copy. Georgia has no statute on trespass notices specific to rental housing.

title: No Crime-Free Lease or Police-Cooperation Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, landlord cooperation with police, or penalties for tenants who call for help.
