A lease may bar serious misconduct and criminal acts, and ending a lease for violating such a term is not retaliation. A tenant protected by a family violence or stalking order may end the lease early, and a copy of the order goes to you with the notice, plus the police report if the order is an ex parte temporary protective order. One reporting duty does reach you: anyone who knows of a death by violence, suicide or casualty, a sudden death of someone in apparent good health, a suspicious or unusual death, an apparent drug overdose, or a death unattended by a physician (as the statute defines it) must immediately notify the coroner or county medical examiner, and anyone who knows of the death of a child must immediately notify the coroner or medical examiner (O.C.G.A. §§ 45-16-24(a), 19-15-3(f)). Reporting child abuse, or abuse of a disabled adult or elder person, is required only of listed professionals, which do not include landlords, though anyone may report (O.C.G.A. §§ 19-7-5(c)-(d), 30-5-4(a)).

title: Notices Georgia Requires in Writing
bodyText: Several Georgia notices must be written: the owner and manager disclosure and its updates (or a conspicuous posting of a change), the escrow account location and the move-in and move-out damage lists (unless you are a small owner exempt from those rules), the deposit retention statement, and a service member's and a family-violence tenant's termination notices. The demand for possession and three-day notice must be posted in a sealed envelope, so they are written too. The tenancy-at-will notice statute does not require writing; give those notices in writing anyway.

title: Who May Appear for an Entity Landlord
bodyText: Georgia lets an employee of a corporation or other legal entity represent it in magistrate court, where most dispossessories are filed. Anyone else appearing for another person or an entity in court must be a licensed attorney: practicing law, or appearing as an attorney for another, without a license is unlawful. The same statute bars a corporation from practicing law, but another section lets a corporation act in matters to which it is a party; how these fit together outside magistrate court is case law. In state or superior court an entity landlord should use a lawyer. A property manager who is not your employee should not appear for you in court; whether a manager or agent may sign the dispossessory affidavit is a question of the court's practice and case law.

title: How Dispossessory Papers Are Served
bodyText: The dispossessory summons and affidavit are served by the sheriff, a constable or an approved process server: personally if possible, otherwise by leaving them with a person of legal age living at the premises, or, if none is found after reasonable effort, by posting them on the door and mailing a copy the same day by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address. Georgia has no rule letting the lease name a person to accept the papers. Posting and mailing supports a default for possession only, not money. A tenant enrolled in the state address confidentiality program designates the Secretary of State for mail and service of process. The program sections read do not address dispossessory service; the cautious course is to serve at the rented premises under the dispossessory rules, and do not ask the program for the tenant's address.

title: Jury Trial Waivers
bodyText: Magistrate courts in Georgia hold no jury trials, and a dispossessory there is tried by the judge; an appeal goes to state or superior court for a new trial. In a court of record, the right to a jury is preserved, and the parties may consent to a trial without a jury by written stipulation filed with the court or by oral stipulation in open court. Whether a jury waiver signed in advance in a residential lease is enforceable is case law, and the dispossessory article itself cannot be waived. The library offers no jury-waiver clause.

title: Leasing to Minors
bodyText: The age of majority in Georgia is 18. A minor's contract, including a lease, is generally voidable, though it binds a minor who keeps the benefit after turning 18, an emancipated minor, and a minor whose parent or guardian failed to supply necessaries such as housing (you must prove that). Georgia has no rule on naming minors as dispossessory defendants or barring filings against them. Lease to an adult, or have an adult co-sign or guarantee.

title: Seasonal Rentals, Hotels and Extended Stays
bodyText: Georgia has no special rules for seasonal or vacation tenancies; a seasonal rental of a dwelling is a residential rental agreement like any other. Hotel, boarding-house and other day-to-day or weekly accommodations are different: the keeper must give a guest notice equal to the paid period before ending occupancy, except for cause. For an innkeeper's guest, a separately signed or initialed written statement in bold type of the occupancy period is a binding contract, after which the guest may be kept out and property moved to a secure place. Whether a long-term hotel stay becomes a tenancy is case law. Local short-term rental ordinances may apply.

title: A Georgia Lease Conveys Only a Usufruct
bodyText: In Georgia a lease of less than five years gives the tenant only a usufruct, the right to possess and use the property, unless the lease expressly says otherwise; no estate passes from you. The tenant's usufruct cannot be conveyed without your consent and cannot be levied on. So in Georgia the word describes the tenant's right, and a tenant may sublet only with your consent. If you hold the home only for life (a life estate) and rent it by the year, a tenant who keeps to the lease may stay for the rest of that year after your estate ends, but no longer.

title: Leases for Prostitution Are Void
bodyText: Georgia voids any lease or rental agreement of a house, building, tourist camp or other structure made for the purpose of prostitution or assignation. A lease used for other illegal purposes is not voided by a landlord-tenant statute; a contract to do an illegal thing is unenforceable under general contract law, and the lease's own prohibited-use and criminal-activity terms are the landlord's tool.

title: When a Georgia Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: A Georgia lease for one year or less may be oral. A lease that is not to be performed within one year of being made must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged or someone lawfully authorized, unless it has been fully performed, performed by one side and accepted by the other, or so far performed that refusing to honor it would be a fraud. An agreement to modify, cancel or release such a lease must be in writing and signed by all parties, unless the party it is enforced against admits in court that it was made. A lease of five years or more, or a shorter one that says so, can pass an estate rather than only a usufruct. Use a written, signed lease for every tenancy.

title: No Special Signing Formalities
bodyText: Georgia sets no special formality for a residential lease: no seal, witness, notary or acknowledgment, and no spouse's consent. A lease that must be in writing (more than a year) needs only the signature of the party to be charged or someone lawfully authorized; an agent who signs a lease that must be in writing should have written authority. Recording a lease is optional.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Georgia has no unconscionability statute for leases of real property. The Commercial Code's unconscionability rules sit in its sales and leases articles, which the library reads as written for goods; courts may apply the doctrine to other contracts as a matter of case law. A contract against public policy cannot be enforced, and the Georgia statutes that bar specific lease terms (repair waivers, one-way attorney fees, waivers of the deposit, dispossessory and distress rules) apply whatever the bargain. Keep terms balanced and plain.

title: Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act and Leases
bodyText: Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act bans unfair or deceptive acts or practices in consumer transactions, and a consumer transaction includes the lease or rental of property, real or personal, primarily for personal, family or household purposes. The act's list has one lease item: when someone buys the home of an owner whose loan is in default and the owner stays on under a lease, the lease must state the monthly rent and, in plain and bold language, that the owner may be evicted for nonpayment. It lists no general residential-lease practices (such as blank spaces or failing to give a copy). A tenant must send a written demand at least 30 days before suing, and an injured consumer may recover damages, treble damages for intentional violations and attorney fees. Whether and how far the act reaches a residential lease may be a question for the courts, so treat it as applying.

title: Georgia's Non-Waivable List
bodyText: Georgia does not make the whole landlord-tenant chapter non-waivable. Instead it lists what a residential lease or similar agreement, oral or written, may not waive, assign, transfer or otherwise avoid: the landlord's repair duty and liability for failure to repair; local housing-code ordinances adopted under the state's enabling statute; the dispossessory procedure; the distress-warrant procedure; the security deposit article; and applicable Civil Practice Act provisions not superseded. The family-violence and service member termination rights cannot be waived either, and a one-way attorney-fee term is void. Other rules may generally be varied by agreement, but laws made for public order or good morals cannot be set aside by agreement, and a right may be waived only where that does not injure others or affect the public interest.

title: Exculpatory and Indemnity Clauses
bodyText: A Georgia residential lease cannot waive or avoid your duty to keep the premises in repair or your liability for damages from defective construction or failure to repair. So a clause releasing you from, or making the tenant indemnify you for, injuries or damage caused by your failure to repair cannot be relied on. Other exculpatory clauses (for example for loss of the tenant's property from theft or weather) are governed by case law. Do not ask the tenant to indemnify you for your own negligence.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on renting the same room or unit to two tenants at once. If you do, the first tenant still holds the right to possess and enjoy the unit under the first lease; the second tenant's claims against you (such as contract or fraud) are case law. Do not sign a new lease until the current tenant has given up possession or a writ has been executed.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules Bind Tenants
bodyText: In a Georgia condominium, everyone entitled to occupy a unit, tenants included, must comply with the lawful provisions of the condominium instruments and the association's reasonable rules that have been provided to the unit owners, and the association may sue for noncompliance. The same duty binds occupants in a planned subdivision of 15 or more lots under its covenants. No Georgia statute found caps association lease approval fees or lets the association collect rent from your tenant. Rules on amending condominium and association instruments may affect new rental restrictions; check the instruments and any amendment's effect on you. Give your tenant the instruments and rules, and keep the lease's association-compliance clause.

title: No Truth in Renting or Tenant Purchase Right
bodyText: Georgia has no Truth in Renting Act, no statutory tenant opportunity to purchase and no tenant right of first refusal on a sale. Nothing requires a statement of tenant rights in or with the lease.

title: No State Tenant Rights Guide
bodyText: Georgia requires no state-published rights and responsibilities guide, handbook or statement of tenant rights before signing or at renewal, and none must be attached to the lease. The Georgia disclosures that do apply are the owner and manager disclosure, the flooding notice, and, unless the small-owner exemption applies, the escrow account location and the move-in damage list.

title: No Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Georgia has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that must be given, acknowledged or attached as the first page of a lease. See No State Tenant Rights Guide.

title: No Month-to-Month Parity Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute barring terms that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or capping the rent difference between them. A tenancy with no end date is a tenancy at will ending on 60 days' notice from you or 30 from the tenant.

title: Tenant Organizing Is Protected From Retaliation
bodyText: Georgia protects a tenant who establishes, tries to establish or takes part in a tenant organization to address habitability problems such as life, health or safety concerns. Filing a dispossessory, cutting services, raising rent, ending the lease or materially interfering with the lease within three months after that activity makes a prima facie case of retaliation, unless a statutory exception applies (for example the tenant is behind on rent). Georgia has no broader statutory right to organize, meet or distribute literature.

title: No State Single-Family Rental Limit
bodyText: Georgia has no statute limiting the rental of homes in single-family zones or requiring the owner to live on the lot. Local zoning, short-term rental ordinances and recorded covenants may restrict rentals; check them for each property. Local governments may not regulate the amount of rent on private residential property.

title: No State Accessory Dwelling Unit Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on accessory dwelling units: none that stops local governments from restricting them, allows them by right, or sets owner-occupancy or minimum-term rules for renting one. Local zoning governs; check it before renting an accessory unit.

title: A Georgia Tenant's Statutory Duties
bodyText: Georgia's statutes give a tenant only a few duties of their own. A tenant has no rights beyond using the property rented and the privileges needed to enjoy that use, and may not cut or destroy growing trees, remove permanent fixtures or otherwise injure the property. The tenant must deliver possession at the end of the term. A tenant in possession may not dispute your title or attorn to another claimant. An occupant who fails to keep a required smoke detector in good working order can be fined up to $25 after a first warning. Other duties, such as cleanliness, rules and notice of defects, come from the lease.

title: Tenant Acts Georgia Law Forbids
bodyText: Georgia has no statutory list of acts a residential tenant must not commit. The acts barred by statute are few: a tenant may not injure the property, cut growing trees or remove permanent fixtures; intentionally damaging another's property (up to $500) or knowingly and maliciously interfering with its use is criminal trespass; and a lease for prostitution is void. Everything else (noise, smoking, pets, guests, alterations) is for the lease.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: Georgia's automatic-renewal statute covers service contracts sold to consumers, not leases of a dwelling, so it does not by its terms govern a lease that renews itself. A lease that renews automatically is a matter of contract. The cautious course is to state any automatic renewal clearly and conspicuously in the lease, and to remind the tenant 30 to 60 days before the date by which they must give notice not to renew. A tenancy with no end date is a tenancy at will instead.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Georgia does not require a residential lease to be recorded. A lease executed with the formalities for a deed may be recorded in the county where the property lies, and the record is then notice of the parties' interests. A tenant in possession also gives notice of their rights by possession. Recording changes no landlord-tenant right.

title: Documents for a Family-Violence or Stalking Termination
bodyText: Georgia has one family-violence provision for tenants, the early-termination right, so there is one list of qualifying documents. The tenant's written notice must come with a copy of a civil family violence order (a protective order under Georgia's family violence law issued after a hearing the respondent attended or had notice of, or an ex parte temporary order with a police report showing a basis for it), a civil stalking order (the same, under the stalking statute), or a criminal family violence or stalking order (a pretrial release order after an arrest, or a probation order after a conviction, plea or first-offender disposition). An ex parte temporary order counts only with the police report. A counselor's or advocate's statement is not enough under Georgia law; federal programs accept other documents.

title: No State Eviction Defense for Victims
bodyText: Georgia law lets a tenant end the lease early when a family violence or stalking order protects the tenant or the tenant's minor child, but no statute bars evicting a tenant because of violence committed against them or calls for help, and no defense to a dispossessory on that ground. In housing under a federal covered housing program (public housing, vouchers, tax-credit and other listed programs), federal law bars evicting a tenant because they are a victim, and an incident of violence against them is not a serious lease violation or good cause. Fair-housing law may also apply. The cautious course: do not end a tenancy because of violence against the tenant.

title: No Statutory Lock-Change Right for Victims
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving a victim of family violence or stalking the right to have the locks changed, and none voiding a lease term against it. A protective order may order the abuser to stop the violence or stalking, and a family violence order may exclude the abuser from the residence; follow any order you are shown. Changing the locks promptly at a protected tenant's request, at the tenant's cost or yours as the lease provides, is the cautious course, and do not give a key to a person an order excludes.

title: Deposit Return After a Family-Violence Termination
bodyText: Georgia has no special deposit rule for a family-violence or stalking termination. The usual rules apply: unless you qualify for the small-owner exemption, within three business days after the lease ends and the premises are vacated or surrendered, inspect and list damage; in every case, return the deposit, less proper deductions with the written statement, within 30 days after obtaining possession. If other tenants on the lease stay, the statute does not say when the departing tenant's share is due; the cautious course is to account to the departing tenant for the deposit when you regain possession of the unit, and to agree in writing how any share is handled if co-tenants remain.

title: Where Georgia's Protective-Order Statutes Are
bodyText: The termination statute's cross-references are current. Family violence protective orders are issued under Article 1 of Chapter 13 of Title 19 (the family violence article, beginning with its definition of family violence), and stalking protective orders under the stalking statute in Title 16. Neither has been moved or renumbered. Family violence protective orders may grant a party possession of the residence and exclude or evict the other party; stalking orders may bar stalking, harassing or interfering but do not list possession. Both are effective statewide and enforced by law enforcement.

title: Georgia's Address Confidentiality Program
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, Georgia's Secretary of State runs a victim-centered address confidentiality program. A participant gets a card with a designated address and the office serves as their agent for mail and service of process. Government bodies must use the designated address when asked; a private landlord is not listed among the entities asked to use it, but honoring a tenant's request to send mail to the designated address is the cautious course. Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to keep a victim's information confidential; keep it private anyway, and limit who sees an order or police report a tenant gives you.

title: No Sex-Offender Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Georgia does not require a landlord to tell tenants or applicants about registered sex offenders nearby or in the building, and no lease notice about the registry is required. The state registry is public; you may point tenants to it. What you need not disclose about the property is covered in What a Landlord Need Not Disclose.

title: Sex-Offender Residency Restrictions
bodyText: Georgia bars a registered sex offender whose offense occurred on or after July 1, 2008 from residing within 1,000 feet of a child care facility, church, school or area where minors congregate. The duty is the offender's, not the landlord's: no Georgia statute makes it a crime to lease to an offender or to two offenders living together. A tenant who claims an exemption because the facility arrived later, or the lease began before July 1, 2008, proves it with the lease, and a lease exemption lasts only for the term of the executed lease. Screening policies on criminal history must still meet fair-housing law.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a building to condominiums (a conversion condominium created on or after July 1, 1980), you must give each residential tenant in possession who is not in default notice of the conversion at least 120 days before requiring them to leave, setting out generally their rights. During those 120 days the tenant may be required to leave only for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants, and the tenancy terms may not change. Within 60 days of the notice you must offer to sell the unit to the tenant at a stated price and terms, with the condominium disclosure items, the tenant has 60 days to accept, and if the tenant does not, for 120 days after the offer you may not offer the unit to others on better terms without first offering those terms to the tenant, who has at least ten days to accept. A notice that names a vacate date is also a demand for possession. The act does not let you end a lease early in breach of its terms. No special first clause or capital-letter statement is required in the lease.

title: A Tenant's Unpaid Utility Bills and Your Property
bodyText: A Georgia public or private water supplier may not put a lien on your property for water charges unless you, the owner, incurred them, and the same rule applies to suppliers of gas, sewer service and electricity. A water supplier may not refuse service to a separately metered unit for a new owner or tenant because a prior owner or occupant owes it money. No lease clause or affidavit is needed for this protection. If you hold the utility account yourself, the charges are yours. You or a tenant may request a statement of water charges owed for the property.

title: No Pest-Control Notice Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring notice to tenants before pesticide application or extermination in a rental, and none assigning pest control between landlord and tenant. Your duty to keep the premises in repair and fit for human habitation is the background rule, and the lease can allocate routine pest control. Licensed applicators follow their own pesticide rules.

title: No Bed Bug Cooperation Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a tenant to cooperate with bed bug inspection or treatment, or setting who pays. The lease can require the tenant to report pests, allow entry for treatment and prepare the unit, and your repair and fitness duty still applies. See No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule.

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals: nothing requires you to allow them or limits the insurance or deposit you may require. The lease decides; any added refundable deposit counts toward the two-month deposit cap.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on smart locks, keypad or app-based entry systems in rentals: no rule on data they collect, on offering a physical key, or on cutting off another person's access for a victim of violence. The lease and the entry provisions govern.

title: No Government-Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: Georgia has no statute delaying rent or eviction for a federal or state employee during a government shutdown or furlough. The ordinary rules apply, including the tenant's tender defense, which you are required to accept only once in any 12-month period.

title: The Ten-Unit Exemption
bodyText:
Georgia's deposit law has one portfolio-size threshold. A natural person who, with a spouse and minor children, owns ten or fewer rental units is exempt from the escrow account, surety bond, move-in and move-out damage list and penalty sections of the deposit law, but only if no third person manages the units, including collecting rent, for a fee. Both conditions must be met. The exemption never reaches the deposit cap or the 30-day return and wear-and-tear rules.

Georgia's fair housing article also has size-based exemptions: apart from its advertising rule, its ban on discrimination in selling and renting does not reach a single-family home rented by a private owner who owns no more than three such homes and rents without a broker or discriminatory advertising, or rooms or units in an owner-occupied dwelling for no more than four families. No other Georgia landlord duty found is tiered by portfolio size.

title: No State Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring you to give tenants health-department rental regulations or to refer them to a health district. County boards of health and local housing codes may set rules for rental housing; check locally.

title: No Staff Screening Rule for Senior Housing
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring work cards or background checks for staff of 55-and-older or other senior rental housing. Licensed care facilities such as assisted living have their own licensing rules, which are outside an ordinary lease.

title: Housing an Employee or Caretaker
bodyText: Georgia's dispossessory procedure applies to croppers and servants who keep possession after their employment ends, in the same way as to tenants, so the cautious course is to remove a caretaker or employee you housed by dispossessory, not self-help. Georgia has no statute requiring a signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating terms for employee housing, or a filing for guest-worker housing. Put the housing terms, and what happens when the job ends, in writing.

title: Liens for a Tenant's Improvements
bodyText: A Georgia contractor's or supplier's lien attaches to the owner's real estate when the work or materials are furnished at the instance of the owner, the contractor, or someone acting for the owner or contractor. Whether a tenant ordering work counts as acting for you, for example because the lease requires or consents to the work, is for the courts. Georgia has no statute letting a lease clause keep your interest free of liens for tenant work. Require written approval of any alteration and proof that contractors were paid.

title: Cannabis in Georgia Rentals
bodyText:
No Georgia statute protects a medical cannabis or low-THC oil registrant from being refused a lease or penalized for that status, and none limits a lease ban on cannabis. Marijuana possession, cultivation and sale outside the state's medical cannabis program for registered patients are crimes under Georgia's Controlled Substances Act, so a lease may bar them as illegal use, and a lease may ban smoking of any substance.

How the registered-patient exception works is set by the medical cannabis and registry statutes; check them before acting against a registered patient.

title: No Statute on Which Appliances You Supply
bodyText: Georgia has no statute presuming that appliances in the unit are landlord-supplied, requiring a stove or refrigerator, or barring a lease from excluding them. The lease decides what is included. The cautious course is to treat appliances you supply as part of the premises you must keep in repair, so list them, and list any you are not responsible for.

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText: Georgia law does not require a landlord to provide a stove or refrigerator. See No Statute on Which Appliances You Supply.

title: No Duty to Provide Alternate Housing
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a private landlord to provide or pay for alternate housing while the unit is repaired or after a casualty. A fire or other casualty not caused by you does not by statute abate the rent; the lease decides that. Relocation assistance in Georgia law is for people displaced by public acquisitions.

title: Smoke Detector Tampering and Fees
bodyText: Georgia puts the duty to keep a required smoke detector in good working order on the occupant: an occupant who fails to do so faces a fine of up to $25 after a first warning. No statute authorizes, or caps, a lease fee for removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm. A fixed charge is an agreed-damages term; whether it binds or is a penalty is for the courts, so tie any charge to your actual cost of replacing or resetting the device. Failing to maintain a detector is not evidence of negligence in a damages case.

title: Firearm Rules in a Georgia Lease
bodyText:
No Georgia statute bars or limits a private landlord's lease term restricting firearms in the unit or common areas, and none protects a tenant's possession of firearms in a rental. State law preempts local regulation of firearm possession and carrying, so a city or county cannot impose such rules, but that preemption reaches governments, not private contracts.

A separate statute limits employers searching employees' locked cars for firearms; it applies to employer parking lots, not tenant parking.

Public housing is different: Georgia's Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to require, as a condition of tenancy in public housing, any prohibition or restriction of lawful firearm possession within a dwelling unless federal law requires it.

title: No Statutory Guest Rights
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving tenants' guests or service providers a right of access or barring a guest fee. The lease's guest policy governs, within fair-housing law and the criminal-trespass rules for common areas.

title: No Right to Run a Child Care Home
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to allow a tenant to operate a family child care home, or limiting a lease term that bars one. The lease's use clause governs, and a child care operation may need a state license. Child care facilities near the home can matter for registered sex offenders (see Sex-Offender Residency Restrictions) and lead-hazard rules for pre-1978 housing.

title: Georgia's Fire and Building Codes
bodyText: Georgia runs two code regimes. The state minimum standard codes (the International Building, Residential, Fire, Property Maintenance and other ICC codes and the National Electrical Code) are set by the Department of Community Affairs, as the codes existed on July 1, 2004 unless the department adopts a later edition. The Existing Building and Property Maintenance codes, and any other code the board adds, apply only where a city or county adopts them; the building, residential, fire, fuel gas, mechanical, plumbing, energy and electrical codes apply statewide. The Georgia State Fire Code is adopted separately by the Safety Fire Commissioner, and the minimum codes may not be less restrictive. So the edition that reaches a rental depends on which regime and which rule; check the current adoption before relying on a model-code section. For an ordinary rental the rule met most often is the smoke detector statute: every dwelling unit needs an approved smoke detector (battery units allowed in buildings built before July 1, 1987) at the access to each sleeping area and on each story.

title: Passing Tax Increases to the Tenant
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a tax-escalation clause to state the tenant's exact share or to refund abatements. A written lease may raise rent under an escalation clause for utilities, taxes or insurance, and an increase under such a clause is not retaliation. Use the library's Rent Escalation clause, state the base year and the tenant's share, and pass along any refund of taxes you received for the same period.

title: Agreements for the Tenant to Do Repairs
bodyText: A Georgia residential lease cannot waive, assign or transfer your duty to keep the premises in repair. So you may not shift that duty to the tenant, even by a good-faith agreement or in exchange for lower rent. A tenant may still agree to routine care that is not a repair of the premises, such as yard care or changing filters and light bulbs, and must pay for damage the tenant causes. The library offers no tenant-repair clause for Georgia.

title: Tenant Screening in Georgia
bodyText: Georgia has no tenant-screening statute: no limits on criminal-history look-back periods, no conditional-offer rule, no income-ratio rule and no screening-fee cap. Federal law governs the use of consumer reports: if you take adverse action, such as denying the application, based in whole or in part on a report, you must give the applicant notice and the disclosures the federal statute lists. Screening criteria must also satisfy federal and Georgia fair-housing law, so apply written criteria the same way to every applicant.

title: No Rent-Ledger or Data-Security Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to keep or produce a rent ledger, to include one with a nonpayment notice, or to answer a tenant's records request. No Georgia statute imposes a written information-security program on landlords holding applicants' Social Security numbers or bank data. A nonpayment dispossessory still requires a notice to vacate or pay all past-due rent, late fees, utilities and other charges within three business days, and an affidavit sworn to the facts, so keep an accurate ledger, and limit and secure the personal data you collect.

title: No Statute on Disclosing Tenant Information
bodyText: Georgia has no statute barring a landlord from disclosing a tenant's or applicant's information, or requiring consent first. Federal law limits how you obtain and use consumer reports. The cautious course: share tenant information only with the tenant's consent, under legal process, or as the lease and law require, and keep any family-violence order or police report a tenant gives you private.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on reporting rent payments to credit bureaus: no required positive rent reporting, no ban on requiring enrollment, and no state notice before reporting late rent. If you furnish information to a consumer reporting agency, federal furnisher rules on accuracy and disputes may apply.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet Requirement
bodyText: Georgia does not require a landlord to give a state fact sheet on pets and eviction. Belongings removed under a writ, pets included, are treated as abandoned after execution, so a tenant with animals should plan for them before the writ is executed; contact animal control if an animal is left behind.

title: No Statute on Residential Parking Rules
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on residential parking rules in a lease: no prescribed heading or delivery before signing, no limit on mid-term changes or on vehicle data you request, and no rule unbundling parking from rent. Towing from private property is regulated separately (see Towing Vehicles from Rental Property). Put parking terms in the lease or written rules.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring parking to be priced separately from rent or barring a parking charge. See No Statute on Residential Parking Rules.

title: No Veteran Rental Incentive
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving landlords a tax credit or other incentive for renting to veterans, and none requiring a veteran discount.

title: No Tenant Display Rights Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving tenants a right to display flags, political signs or religious items, or limiting a lease restriction on them. The lease's rules govern, within fair-housing law (rules that target a religion are discriminatory).

title: No Religious Display Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving tenants a right to place religious or cultural items on doors or doorframes. See No Tenant Display Rights Statute.

title: No Canvasser Access Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to let candidates or canvassers into an apartment building, or barring a no-solicitation policy. Common-area access is controlled by the lease and the criminal-trespass rules.

title: No State Cable or Satellite Access Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on cable or satellite access in rental buildings or barring a rent difference for subscribers. Federal rules on over-the-air reception devices may limit restrictions on a tenant's own dish in areas the tenant controls.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a tenant moves in. Treat hot water equipment you supply as part of your repair duty. A scalding setting could support a negligence claim.

title: No Emergency-Contact Notice Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a lease or posting to give tenants a management website, an after-hours emergency number or a social-services hotline. The owner and manager disclosure is required (see Owner and Manager Disclosure); giving an emergency maintenance contact is good practice.

title: No Penalty for Using a Void Lease Term
bodyText: Georgia has no statute penalizing a landlord for knowingly putting a prohibited term in a lease. A one-way attorney-fee term is void and a waiver of the repair duty cannot be relied on, and misleading lease terms could be argued as a deceptive practice under the Fair Business Practices Act.

title: Code Inspections of Rental Property
bodyText: Georgia limits local inspections of residential rental property: a local government may inspect or investigate only with probable cause to believe a code violation exists or has existed (a violation in plain view counts), and it may never require registration of residential rental property. Where a licensed broker manages the property, the tenant must give a code officer the manager's name, license number and contact information on request. A local unfit-building ordinance may authorize the public officer to enter premises for examinations, with the least possible inconvenience to those in possession. No Georgia statute lets a lease itself authorize an inspector's entry without the tenant's consent.

title: When a Local Government Declares a Building Unfit
bodyText: Georgia counties and cities may adopt ordinances to order unfit dwellings repaired, closed or demolished, with notice to interested parties, persons in possession included, and a court hearing. If the owner does not comply, the public officer may close the building and post a placard stating that its use or occupation 'is prohibited and unlawful'. Georgia has no statute expressly barring rent after a condemnation or vacate order, but a tenant cannot lawfully occupy a closed building, your repair and fitness duties cannot be waived, and unfit-dwelling ordinances adopted under the urban redevelopment law's repair-and-demolition section cannot be waived in a lease. Do not collect rent for a period when occupancy is prohibited.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Orders
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring you to give applicants or tenants copies of outstanding inspection, code-violation or condemnation orders. A tenant in possession is an interested party who must be served in an unfit-building case, and a closed building is placarded. A broker you engage must timely disclose to prospective tenants the broker works with the adverse material facts about the property's physical condition that the broker actually knows and that a reasonably diligent inspection by the tenant would not reveal. Disclosing a known order before signing helps avoid later fraud and fitness claims.

title: No Housing-Code Receivership Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute letting a local government or tenants have a receiver collect rents to repair a substandard rental. Local unfit-building ordinances work instead through repair, closing or demolition orders, with the cost becoming a lien. Courts may appoint a receiver in equity to hold assets charged with paying debts when they are in manifest danger of loss, but that general power is not a housing-code program.

title: Losing the Deposit for Missing the Lists
bodyText:
Georgia ties a hard penalty to the move-in and move-out lists. If you fail to provide the lists and written statements within the deposit statute's deadlines, you forfeit the right to withhold any part of the deposit and the right to sue the tenant for damage to the premises. You also may not keep any part of the deposit if it was not escrowed or bonded, the move-in list was not made and presented, and the final list was not made available.

A tenant who was present for the move-out inspection and signed your final list, or did not dissent specifically, cannot recover, but only if your lists carry written notice of the tenant's duty to sign or dissent; a tenant who was not present and did not ask for a copy of the final list may still dispute it. An owner who is a natural person and who, with a spouse and minor children, owns ten or fewer rental units is exempt from these sections, unless a third party is paid to manage the unit.

title: The Fitness Promise Is Built Into Every Lease
bodyText: Every Georgia residential lease, oral or written, entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024 is deemed to include a provision that the premises are fit for human habitation, so the lease need not state it; treat older leases the same way. You must also keep the premises in repair. Neither duty can be waived. The landlord-tenant statutes do not list what fitness requires. The state's unfit-building law lists conditions a local officer may find make a dwelling unfit (such as fire hazards, poor ventilation, light or sanitation, disrepair, structural defects and uncleanliness), but only for local enforcement; local housing codes and case law fill in the rest.

title: Habitability Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Georgia residential lease cannot waive, assign, transfer or avoid your duty to keep the premises in repair, your liability for failing to repair, the built-in fitness promise, or certain local unfit-dwelling ordinances. Georgia has no statute letting a tenant accept listed defects for a rent reduction. Do not rely on a lease term that tries any of these; the statute says it may not be done.

title: No Modifiable Habitability List
bodyText: Georgia's statute states the fitness and repair duties generally and lists no specific conditions (water, heat, hot water and so on) that a lease may modify for particular premises. Nothing in the duty can be waived. Where a home has no utility or well water, describe what is and is not supplied in the lease, but do not agree that an unfit condition is acceptable.

title: No Statutory Materiality Test
bodyText: Georgia's statutes do not say how serious a defect must be to breach the fitness promise or repair duty, or what the tenant must show; those tests are case law. Treat any defect that affects health, safety or basic use as urgent.

title: No Statutory Habitability Presumption
bodyText: Georgia has no statute presuming a unit unfit (or fit) under the lease's fitness promise. In a local unfit-building case, a health department, health officer or building inspector's finding that private property is a health or safety hazard is prima-facie evidence of a violation. One related rule: in a retaliation claim, a code-compliance inspection within the prior 12 months is a rebuttable defense for you.

title: Habitability Rules Georgia Does Not Have
bodyText: Georgia's habitability law is short: a non-waivable duty to keep the premises in repair, a built-in promise of fitness, liability for damage from defective construction or failure to repair, a ban on knowingly and willfully cutting off cooling, heat, light or water before a dispossessory is finally decided, and smoke detectors. It has no statewide list of minimum habitability conditions for leases (the unfit-building law lists conditions only for local enforcement), no heat or hot-water temperature rule, no repair-and-deduct or rent-escrow remedy, no repair deadlines, and no rent abatement by statute; local codes and case law may supply some of these.

title: No Statewide Heat Standard
bodyText: Georgia has no statute setting a minimum indoor temperature or barring a lease from making the tenant pay for heat. Treat heating equipment you supply as part of your repair duty and the fitness promise, and you may not knowingly and willfully cut off heat before a dispossessory is finally decided. Who pays for fuel or electricity is for the lease.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to the Tenant
bodyText: A Georgia residential lease cannot shift your repair duty to the tenant, whatever consideration is given. The lease may make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant causes and for routine care that is not a repair of the premises; where routine care ends and repair begins is case law, not reviewed. See Agreements for the Tenant to Do Repairs.

title: Promises to Repair Before Signing
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring your promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing with a completion date. But a lease of more than a year, and any change to it, must be in writing, and an oral promise outside a written lease is hard to prove. Put any promised work and its date in the lease or a signed addendum.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring you to name a person to receive repair requests or letting the tenant choose a repairer. You must disclose who manages the property and the service agent (Owner and Manager Disclosure).

title: Tenant Remedies for Failure to Repair
bodyText: Georgia's statutes give a tenant no repair-and-deduct right, no rent escrow and no court-ordered repair procedure. What they do give: your liability for damages from failure to repair, which cannot be waived; the right to raise your breach as a defense or counterclaim in a dispossessory; protection from retaliation for asking for repairs or complaining to code officials; and local code enforcement. Other remedies come from case law.

title: No Statutory Repair-Request Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring repair requests to be written or setting what notice the tenant must give. A tenant's notice to repair is a protected act for retaliation purposes. When your liability depends on knowing of a defect is case law; a lease term asking for written requests helps you respond but does not cut off claims based on what you otherwise knew.

title: No Repair-Cost Termination Right
bodyText: Georgia has no statute letting a landlord end a lease because repairs would cost too much, or letting a tenant end it for an unrepaired defect. The lease's casualty clause governs damage from fire or other casualty; otherwise the repair duty continues.

title: No Rent Escrow for Repairs
bodyText: Georgia has no rent-escrow procedure for repairs, so there is no escrow exemption or exemption notice. Rent paid into court in Georgia arises only in a dispossessory.

title: Which Code Edition an Older Building Must Meet
bodyText: For local unfit-building enforcement, Georgia measures a building against the building or minimum standard codes in existence when the improvement was constructed, unless another law provides otherwise. Housing and property maintenance standards adopted by ordinance, and the state fire and life-safety codes, are not limited that way. So an older rental is not required by that statute to meet today's construction code, but must meet current maintenance and safety rules.

title: No Code-Variance Notice Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a housing or health-code variance, waiver or exception to be given to tenants or attached to the lease. Disclose any variance that affects the unit's condition.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Terms Can Be Agreed
bodyText:
In Georgia the destruction of the unit by fire, or loss of possession through a casualty not caused by you, does not abate the rent the lease sets, and that rule is not on the non-waivable list, so the lease may provide for termination or abatement after a casualty (the library's clause does).

The general duty to lessen damages after a breach is also not on the list; whether a lease may waive it is case law, and the deposit statute separately requires you to attempt to mitigate before keeping deposit money for damages.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving a landlord or tenant a right to end a lease after an environmental event such as flooding, contamination or a declared disaster. Rent is not abated by a casualty unless the lease says so; use the casualty clause.

title: No Disaster Rule for Tenancies
bodyText: Georgia has no statute ending a tenancy or suspending rent after a declared natural disaster, or setting landlord duties when a unit is inaccessible. A casualty not caused by you does not abate rent unless the lease provides it, and your repair duty continues.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText:
Georgia's Fair Housing Act requires reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when needed to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, and requires you to permit reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense. For a rental you may, where reasonable, condition a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at the end, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Georgia does not require that condition to be in the lease and has no restoration-deposit rule of its own.

Federal rules bar raising the usual security deposit for a tenant with a disability, but let you negotiate, where needed, payments into an interest-bearing escrow account, with the interest going to the tenant, not exceeding the restoration cost. Whether those payments count toward Georgia's two-month deposit cap is not settled by statute; the cautious course is to keep the deposit and any restoration payments within two months' rent.

Multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991 must meet the accessible-design requirements.

title: Children and Familial Status
bodyText: Georgia's fair housing article bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, or advertising a preference because of familial status, which under the federal definition covers households with children under 18. Federal law exempts qualifying housing for older persons from the familial-status rules. Georgia does not require the lease to address children's occupancy, and its only familial-status rule for a tenancy that changes (a child born or arriving during the lease) is the general ban on discrimination in terms and conditions. Federal law preserves reasonable government limits on the number of occupants; any limit you set yourself should be reasonable and applied to everyone; the small-owner exemptions do not cover discriminatory advertising.

title: Questions and Advertising About Protected Traits
bodyText: Georgia has no separate statute banning questions about protected traits or records of them. Its Fair Housing Act does make it unlawful to make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin, and that rule applies even to owners otherwise exempt. Asking about a protected trait can be evidence of discrimination, so do not ask except to process an accommodation request.

title: Student Housing
bodyText: Georgia has no student-housing rule for private rentals: no exemption from tenant protections and no special duties. Housing authorities may build and run University System dormitories under a separate financing statute. A private lease to students is an ordinary residential lease; a student under 18 is a minor (see Leasing to Minors).

title: No Smoke-Free Housing Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute making apartment common areas or units smoke-free, or addressing smoke drift between units. A lease smoking policy governs; Smoke that seriously interferes with another tenant's use could support a nuisance claim under general law.

title: No Drug-Free Housing Program Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute creating a drug- and alcohol-free housing category or prescribing its lease terms. A lease may bar illegal drug activity as a serious-misconduct term, and ending a lease for violating it is not retaliation. Federally assisted housing has its own drug-related termination rules.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Lease
bodyText: Georgia has no communal, tribal or clan land tenure and no rule requiring a government officer to approve a residential lease. Leases of state-owned lands and public property have their own approval statutes, which do not reach private rentals.

title: No Initials or Signature-Line Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a tenant to initial particular lease terms for them to bind, for example a notice period longer than the law requires. Initials are good evidence the tenant saw a term. Georgia uses separate signing or initials elsewhere, not for leases: an innkeeper's bold-type statement of a guest's occupancy period binds when separately signed or initialed by the guest, and the arbitration code does not reach an arbitration clause in a residential real estate sale or loan agreement, or an employment contract, unless all signatories initial it.

title: No Font or Placement Rules for Disclosures
bodyText: Georgia sets no font size, bold type or first-page placement for residential lease disclosures. The disclosures it requires (owner and manager, flooding, escrow location, move-in list) have content and timing rules, not layout rules.

title: No Minimum Type Size
bodyText: Georgia has no statute setting a minimum type size for a residential lease. Use a readable size anyway; terms a court finds hidden may be read against you.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Georgia has no plain-language statute that reaches residential leases: no readability test, captioned sections or front-page statement of landlord-protective terms. Write plainly anyway; a court may read an unclear term against you.

title: No Statement of Consumer Restrictions
bodyText: Georgia requires no statement listing the waivers or restrictions in a consumer lease and has no Attorney General plain-language approval. See No Plain-Language Lease Law.

title: No Translation Duty
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a lease to be translated when you advertise or negotiate in another language, and no prescribed verbatim lease text. If you negotiate in another language, offering a translation helps show the tenant understood the terms.

title: What a Georgia Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Georgia prescribes very little lease content and no first-page rule. You must disclose in writing the owner of record or service agent and the manager; give the flooding notice before signing where it applies; tell the tenant in writing where the deposit is escrowed (unless exempt or you post a surety bond instead); give a signed move-in damage list before taking a deposit (unless exempt); and give the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing. Start and end dates belong in the lease as good practice; a tenancy without an end date is a tenancy at will.

title: Georgia's Required Lease Disclosures and Their Timing
bodyText:
At or before the start of the tenancy: the owner (or service agent) and manager names and addresses, in writing.

Before signing a written lease, where flooding has damaged the living space at least three times in the five years before the lease: the written flooding notice.

With the deposit: written notice of the escrow account location (the statute sets no time; none is needed if you post a surety bond instead), and a signed move-in damage list before the deposit is tendered (both unless exempt).

For pre-1978 housing: the federal lead disclosure before the tenant is obligated.

Georgia requires no statement of tenant rights, no just-cause or rent-law coverage notice, and no state form as the first page. A lease with an option to buy does not by statute trigger a seller disclosure form.

title: Leases With an Option to Purchase
bodyText: Georgia has no statute making a landlord who grants an option to purchase a seller who must give a transfer disclosure statement before the lease is signed. An option to buy land must be in writing and signed. Whether a lease-option is treated as a sale for other purposes is case law. The lease-purchase (rent-to-own) statute deals with leased items.

title: No Tenant Right to Purchase
bodyText: Georgia has no tenant opportunity-to-purchase or right-of-first-offer law for rentals, so there is no notice to give before selling. The one tenant purchase right is the offer a condominium converter must make to tenants.

title: No Purchase-Right Exemption Notice
bodyText: Because Georgia has no tenant purchase right or rent-cap act, there is no exemption notice to give. See No Tenant Right to Purchase.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant-Protection Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no core tenant-protection statute on a dated repeal clock. One dated change to note: the dispossessory notice section has a new version effective January 1, 2027 (adding sealing of records), and the address confidentiality program took effect July 1, 2026.

title: No State Rule on Late Fees for Subsidized Rent
bodyText: Georgia has no statute barring a late fee on the part of rent a housing subsidy pays. Federal program rules and the housing assistance contract govern; follow them.

title: Voucher Inspections and Georgia Law
bodyText: Georgia has no source-of-income rule (see No Statewide Source-of-Income Rule) and no statute on refusing a voucher tenancy because of the program inspection. Local ordinances may differ; federal program rules govern once you participate.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute prorating rent, including a subsidy's share, when part of a unit is uninhabitable. A casualty does not abate rent unless the lease provides it; federal program rules may abate the subsidy for failed inspections.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia requires no pre-signing disclosure of nearby former ordnance sites, a pending demolition permit, or shared gas or electric meters. Disclose known conditions that would matter to a tenant anyway.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia requires no lease disclosure for property near a military installation or in a noise or accident-potential zone, and gives no termination right for one. A separate statute bars certain foreign-adversary-linked persons, entities and governments from acquiring any possessory interest, which can include a lease, in land within ten miles of a military base, installation or airport; it does not apply to residential property, defined as real estate intended to be used as the purchaser's dwelling. Check it before leasing such land to a business entity.

title: No Shoreline Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia requires no shoreline, beach or marshland disclosure in a residential lease. Coastal permitting rules apply to owners and development, not to lease terms.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia has no defective or corrosive drywall statute and no disclosure duty for it. A known defect affecting health or fitness is part of your repair duty.

title: Asbestos Rules Do Not Require Tenant Notice
bodyText: The search found Georgia's asbestos law requiring licensed contractors for abatement work and notice of abatement projects to the state; it found no notice to tenants and no lease disclosure. Asbestos that makes the unit unfit falls under your repair duty.

title: No Contamination Disclosure in Leases
bodyText: Georgia requires no environmental-covenant or brownfield statement in a residential lease. But a broker engaged by a landlord must timely disclose to prospective tenants the broker is working with all adverse material facts about the property's physical condition actually known to the broker, environmental contamination included, that a reasonably diligent inspection would not reveal, and known adverse physical conditions within one mile that the tenant could not discover by diligent inspection of the neighborhood or from readily available public records; the brokerage act also preserves any duty the landlord itself has under other law. Disclose known contamination.

title: No Common-Area Lighting Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on common-area lighting in small buildings or on billing a tenant for common-area lights on the tenant's meter. Local security standards may require lighting; put any billing arrangement in the lease.

title: No Balcony Inspection Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks or other exterior elevated elements. Your repair duty and liability for failure to repair cover them.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on steam radiator covers or a related lease rider.

title: No Key-Control Statute
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a key-control policy or employee background checks for apartment complexes. Counties and cities may set minimum security standards for rental dwellings; check local codes.

title: No Apartment Employee Screening Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring background screening of apartment employees.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to test a private well or give tenants results. Treat water you supply as within the fitness promise.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants how to recycle. Local solid-waste ordinances may.

title: No Tenant Right to a Cooling Device
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving tenants a right to install a portable or window air conditioner, or requiring a lease restriction to be disclosed. If you supply cooling, treat it as part of your repair duty, and, for leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024, you may not knowingly and willfully cut off cooling before a dispossessory is finally decided (treat older leases the same way).

title: No Tenant Solar Device Right
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving a tenant a right to install a plug-in solar device or voiding lease restrictions on solar equipment.

title: No Chemical Warning Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring warnings to tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm.

title: No Utility-Transfer Cutoff Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute letting a landlord cut off landlord-name utilities a tenant failed to transfer. A landlord may not knowingly and willfully suspend cooling, heat, light or water before a dispossessory is finally decided; require the transfer in the lease and treat a failure as a lease breach.

title: Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed
bodyText: Georgia's foreclosure statutes give tenants no notice, no right to stay and no rent rule; they regulate notice to the debtor and the sale. Federal law fills the gap for a bona fide tenant: the buyer at foreclosure takes subject to the lease for the rest of its term (except that the successor may end the lease on selling the unit to a purchaser who will live there as a primary residence, still on 90 days' notice), and must give at least 90 days' notice to vacate, also to a tenant at will. A tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant is not the mortgagor or the mortgagor's child, spouse or parent, the deal was at arm's length, and the rent is not substantially below market (unless subsidized). The surety bond in lieu of escrow covers deposits on foreclosure. After the federal notice runs, the cautious course is to use the dispossessory procedure, which covers tenants at will or sufferance; whether a foreclosure buyer may use it against a former tenant is case law, not reviewed.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Pending Foreclosure
bodyText: Georgia does not require you to tell new tenants or applicants that the property is in foreclosure. Federal law protects a bona fide tenant after a sale. Hiding a known foreclosure from a new tenant can still support a fraud or deceptive-practice claim, so disclose it.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on requiring renter's insurance: no rule that the tenant picks the carrier, no limit on force-placed coverage or fees, and no required advisory that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings. A requirement is a lease term. Treat any charge for coverage you place as an agreed lease charge and keep it reasonable (no statute sets a limit); tell tenants in writing that your policy does not cover their property.

title: No Statute on Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on how a tenant's or landlord's insurance claims interact with the lease, such as subrogation waivers or using the tenant's policy for damage the tenant caused. The lease governs; the tenant is liable for damage the tenant causes.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Georgia does not require a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, and local governments may not require rental registration, so there is no registration-linked insurance rule.

title: Out-of-State Owners: Agents and Brokers
bodyText: Georgia has no income-tax withholding duty on rent a tenant pays to a nonresident owner found in these searches, and no rule that a nonresident must name an in-state agent in each lease before suing. What applies: every landlord must disclose the owner of record or a person authorized to receive process and notices, and the manager; and a nonresident owner of single-family or duplex rentals must employ a Georgia-licensed broker (see Out-of-State Owners Must Use a Georgia Broker). If you own through an out-of-state LLC or corporation, it must get a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State before transacting business in Georgia, and until it does it cannot bring an eviction or other court case, though its contracts stay valid and it can defend a case (O.C.G.A. §§ 14-11-702, 14-11-711, 14-2-1501, 14-2-1502). Owning property, without more, is not transacting business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts. An LLC that needs a certificate but has no registered agent here can be served through the Secretary of State, and a foreign corporation with no registered agent can be served by mail to its officers, with a copy to the Secretary of State (O.C.G.A. §§ 14-11-703(h), 14-2-1510(b)). Owning property in Georgia lets Georgia courts hear claims arising from that ownership (O.C.G.A. § 9-10-91). Two tax rules reach nonresident owners. A partnership, S corporation or LLC that owns property in Georgia must withhold Georgia income tax at 4 percent from each nonresident member's share of its Georgia income, unless it files a composite return or another exception applies (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-129). And when a nonresident sells Georgia real property, the buyer generally must withhold 3 percent of the price (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-128).

title: Changing Terms of a Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on how much notice a landlord must give to change rent, fees or other terms of a month-to-month tenancy. A tenancy at will ends on 60 days' notice from you, so the cautious course is to give at least 60 days' written notice of any change, or end the tenancy and offer a new one. A change to a fixed-term lease needs the tenant's agreement, in writing if the lease runs more than a year.

title: Other Rules Georgia Does Not Have
bodyText: Georgia also has no statute on: convenience fees for rent payment methods (its convenience-fee statute covers only listed loan, installment-sale and finance contracts); a cap on returned-check fees beyond the bad-check statute; tenant rights statements or guides; plain-language or type-size rules; translation; rent concessions; double letting; waterbeds; smart locks; and government-shutdown rent relief. Most have their own row with the search behind it; convenience and returned-check fees rest on the statutes' own text, and rent concessions on the search noted for this row.

title: Rules Georgia Has Nowhere in Its Code
bodyText: Searching the whole Official Code, not only the landlord-tenant chapter, Georgia has no state tenant protection at foreclosure (federal law applies), no statute requiring a receipt for cash rent, no landlord registration (local registration is barred, O.C.G.A. § 36-74-30(b); but an out-of-state LLC or corporation transacting business here must register with the Secretary of State and cannot bring an eviction or other court case until it does, O.C.G.A. §§ 14-11-711, 14-2-1502; an unregistered trade name costs you court costs but does not defeat the suit, O.C.G.A. § 10-1-491), no housing-code receivership, no tenant purchase right, and no state source-of-income rule. Squatters are covered by a specific removal statute (see Removing Squatters and Intruders).

title: Nuisance Statutes That Reach Rental Property
bodyText: Georgia defines a nuisance as anything that causes hurt, inconvenience or damage to another that would affect an ordinary, reasonable person, and a superior court may abate a public nuisance. Several statutes reach an owner who leases property used for crime: knowingly leasing a building for sexually related offenses is maintaining a nuisance, with prima facie evidence after repeated incidents noticed in writing by the prosecutor (incidents that result from your cooperation with police do not count); property leased or used by a criminal street gang for gang activity is a public nuisance; and you may not permit premises you own or control to be used for unlawful sale of distilled spirits. A lease for prostitution is void, and a separate nuisance section on substantial drug-related activity on real property also exists. A search found no statute letting a court appoint a receiver or hold rents to abate a nuisance, and no statute requires the lease to summarize a criminal law; act on written notices from prosecutors promptly.

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText: Georgia reads a guaranty strictly: a guarantor's liability is not extended by implication, and an act of yours that increases the guarantor's risk discharges the guarantor. So a guaranty does not automatically cover a renewal, extension, rent increase or other change unless it says so, and a change made without the guarantor's consent may release them. Georgia has no statute requiring a stated maximum or end date, or limiting what a guarantor may be asked to deposit; the two-month cap applies to deposits a tenant gives; the cautious course is to count any deposit a guarantor gives toward it.

title: No Sprinkler Retrofit for Small Rentals
bodyText: Georgia bars the state code, and any local code adopted after May 24, 2010, from requiring fire sprinklers in a single-family dwelling or a residential building of no more than two units. Larger buildings are subject to the state minimum codes and the State Fire Code, including any sprinkler retrofit the fire rules require. Installing, altering or inspecting a sprinkler system is work for a sprinkler contractor that employs a state-certified supervisor full time to do or supervise it; your own staff may repair leaks, replace broken fittings and do routine maintenance that does not change the piping or how the system works.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia requires no lease disclosure of whether a building has fire sprinklers, and has no grant or loan program for private sprinkler retrofits found in these searches. See No Sprinkler Retrofit for Small Rentals.

title: Billing Tenants for Water and Sewer
bodyText: Georgia lets the owner of a residential building submeter or use an allocation method to bill tenants separately for water and sewer. Two conditions: the total charged to all tenants may not exceed what you pay the water system plus a reasonable fee for setting up, servicing and billing, and you must disclose the terms of the charges to the tenant before any contractual agreement, so put them in the lease or an addendum given before signing. Multiunit residential buildings permitted on or after July 1, 2012 must be built to allow per-unit measurement and must bill unit use on measured use, and may allocate common-area use. Georgia has no comparable statute for electric or gas submetering.

title: Charging for Utilities That Are Not Separately Metered
bodyText: For water and sewer, Georgia allows an economic allocation method in place of submeters, capped at your actual cost plus a reasonable billing fee and disclosed before signing; buildings permitted on or after July 1, 2012 must use measured use. Georgia has no statute making a term unenforceable because it charges for other utilities not separately metered; state any allocation formula in the lease.

title: Caps on Rebilled Utility Charges
bodyText: Georgia caps rebilled water and sewer charges at the total you pay the provider plus a reasonable billing fee. No Georgia statute caps rebilled gas or electric charges (see Electric and Gas Submetering).

title: Utility Billing Terms Before Signing
bodyText: Georgia prescribes no utility disclosure attachment or set wording. For separately billed water and sewer, the terms of the charges must be disclosed to the tenant before any contractual agreement; attaching a written statement of how charges are calculated, the billing fee and any common-area allocation does that.

title: Electric and Gas Submetering
bodyText: Georgia has no landlord-tenant statute on reselling electricity or gas to tenants by submeter, and no lease disclosure for it. Whether a landlord who resells electricity is regulated as a utility is a Public Service Commission and Title 46 question; check before reselling.

title: Utility Interruptions in Submetered Buildings
bodyText: Georgia has no special interruption regime for landlord-submetered utilities. The general rule applies: you may not knowingly and willfully cut off cooling, heat, light or water before a dispossessory is finally decided.

title: When the Utility Account Is in Your Name
bodyText: Georgia has no statute letting tenants pay a landlord-held utility bill and deduct it, or petition for a receiver when the landlord does not pay. If the account is yours, the charges are yours, and knowingly and willfully suspending utilities to a tenant before a dispossessory is finally decided is unlawful; whether letting service lapse for your own nonpayment counts is case law, not reviewed, so keep the account paid. A water supplier may not refuse service to a separately metered unit for a new tenant because of a prior occupant's debt.

title: Utility Disconnection Rules
bodyText: Georgia's statutes set no winter or medical moratorium on utility disconnection, and no extra notice. For landlords the rule that matters is the ban on knowingly and willfully cutting off a tenant's utilities before a dispossessory is finally decided.

title: Copying the Landlord on Shutoff Notices
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on authorizing a utility to notify the landlord of a tenant's pending disconnection. A Public Service Commission rule on multi-family dwellings was seen but not reviewed. Ask the tenant to sign the utility's own third-party notice form if one is offered, and require prompt notice in the lease.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on energy-efficiency meter conservation charges passed to tenants. Water and sewer rebilling is capped at cost plus a reasonable billing fee.

title: Claims Against the Property and Attornment
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring you to tell tenants about a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax sale or other proceeding against the property, or requiring tenants to tell you about one. A tenant may not dispute your title or attorn to another claimant while in actual physical occupation, or while otherwise recognizing your title. Federal law protects bona fide tenants after a foreclosure (see Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed).

title: No Tenant Representation in Special Districts
bodyText: Georgia has no statute giving tenants representation or a vote in special service, community improvement or tax allocation districts on account of their tenancy, or requiring a lease notice about them. Passing any district levy through to the tenant is a matter for the lease's tax-escalation terms.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on removing or leaving a tenant-installed EV charger at the end of a tenancy. Treat it as an alteration under the lease: require written approval, licensed installation and either removal with repair or a written agreement that it stays. Georgia gives tenants no right to install one (see No Tenant EV Charging Right).

title: No Rule on Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: Georgia has no statute on EV charging in shared or common parking areas of rental property, or on allocating its cost among tenants. Condominium and association instruments may have their own rules.

title: No Property-Tax Share Statement
bodyText: Georgia does not require a landlord to tell tenants what part of the rent goes to property taxes. A written lease may pass tax increases through an escalation clause (see Passing Tax Increases to the Tenant).

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: Georgia has no statewide rule requiring deadbolts, door viewers or rekeying between tenants. Counties and cities may adopt minimum security standards to prevent unauthorized entry into rental dwellings, not in conflict with fire codes, and may require landlords to comply; check local ordinances. Treat locks you supply as part of your repair duty; rekeying at turnover is the cautious course.

title: No Window Guard or Security Bar Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no statute requiring child window guards or a lease notice about them, and none regulating security or burglar bars on rentals. Bars that cannot be opened from inside can create a fire-exit hazard under the fire and building codes, so check them against local code.

title: Georgia Lead Notices Beyond the Federal Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia requires no state lead notice, certificate or packet to be delivered with the lease; the federal disclosure and pamphlet for pre-1978 housing are the lease-time duties.
