Georgia's notice comes later: when the Department of Public Health determines a lead poisoning hazard exists, it gives written notice, with possible abatement methods, to the owner and everyone living in the dwelling and tries to notify the managing agent; abatement is required when a child under six with confirmed lead poisoning lives in, attends or regularly visits the dwelling (see Lead Poisoning Hazards: Georgia Abatement Duties).

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Leases
bodyText: Georgia requires no lead-safe or lead-free certificate attached to a lease. The state's lead law works through Department of Public Health hazard findings and abatement orders, and a maintenance standard for owners of older housing described in the existing row (see Lead Poisoning Hazards: Georgia Abatement Duties).

title: No Association Disclosure in a Lease
bodyText: Georgia requires condominium disclosures when a unit is first sold, not when it is leased; a lease need not disclose the association's obligations or carry the owner's statement about the condominium law. Tenants must still comply with the condominium instruments and reasonable rules, so give them copies (see Condominium and HOA Rules Bind Tenants).

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Georgia requires no lease disclosure of a certificate of occupancy. Certificates are issued and enforced under the state minimum codes and local enforcement; check that any certificate your local code requires is in place before renting.

title: No Rule on Housing Disaster-Displaced Guests
bodyText: Georgia has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a disaster beyond the lease's guest limits, or barring a landlord from enforcing those limits during an emergency. Use the lease's guest policy, applied fairly.

title: EV Charging Stations You Provide
bodyText: From January 1, 2028, Georgia brings electric vehicle charging stations under the weights-and-measures inspection regime: state inspectors inspect stations, seal those that measure accurately and condemn those that do not, and notify the charging provider, owner or lessee. The regime does not cover a charger at a house or apartment building used other than commercially or reserved for certain people at the property, such as your tenants; a landlord who sells charging to the public should plan for it. Georgia has no statute requiring landlords to install chargers or giving tenants a right to one.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Leased Land
bodyText: In Georgia, a lessee of land may give others permission to hunt on it, as may the landowner or the lessee of the game rights. So unless the lease reserves the hunting and fishing rights, a tenant of rural land may be able to authorize hunters. Use the library's reservation clause if you want to keep those rights.

title: Foreign-Adversary Limits on Land Interests
bodyText: Since July 1, 2024, Georgia bars a nonresident alien tied to a government the U.S. Commerce Secretary designates as a foreign adversary (as the statute defines that term, including certain entities) from acquiring any possessory interest, which can include a lease, in agricultural land or land within ten miles of a military base, military installation or military airport. The ban does not apply to residential property intended as the person's dwelling. An ordinary lease of a home to live in is very likely outside it, though the exception speaks of the purchaser's dwelling; a lease of farmland or of non-residential land near a base to such a person is not.

title: No Home-Business Right for Tenants
bodyText: Georgia has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a rental or limiting a lease restriction on one. The lease's use clause and local zoning govern.

title: Elevators and Other Building Equipment
bodyText: Georgia requires every elevator, escalator, dumbwaiter, manlift and moving walk to be maintained in safe operating condition by the owner or lessee under the state rules, and the enforcement authority notified before any alteration; units erected or placed in service after January 1, 1986 must also be inspected before service and registered within 15 days. Georgia has no product-safety statute putting a separate duty on landlords for facilities such as garage door openers.

title: Pools at Rental Property
bodyText: Georgia's public swimming pool chapter does not apply to apartment complex pools, subdivision pools open only to residents and guests, or a private pool serving a single-family home, and it applies only in counties without their own pool rules in effect on December 31, 2000. A county may adopt pool rules that reach apartment complex pools, so check the county. Georgia has no statewide barrier or lease-notice rule for rental pools; treat a pool you provide as part of the premises you must keep in repair.

title: Misrepresenting a Service Dog
bodyText: Georgia makes it a high and aggravated misdemeanor (fine up to $2,000, up to 30 days, or both) to deliberately misrepresent oneself as qualified to use, train or raise a service dog to obtain accommodations or rights under the state disability-access chapter. That chapter's housing reach is described in Service Dogs: Georgia Penalties and Definitions. The chapter's service-dog definition is described in Service Dogs: Georgia Penalties and Definitions. Emotional support animals are handled as fair-housing reasonable accommodations, and this criminal statute does not let you demand proof beyond what fair-housing law allows.

title: Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Georgia's sales tax reaches rentals of tangible personal property and the services its sales-tax article lists; a dwelling lease is not tangible personal property, so ordinary residential rent carries no state sales tax. Rooms and lodgings furnished by an innkeeper (hotels, motels, inns, campgrounds and online marketplaces facilitating them) may be subject to a local hotel-motel excise tax where the city or county levies one; the tax does not apply to charges for continuous use after the first 30 days of continuous occupancy, and whether a particular short-term rental owes it turns on the innkeeper definition and the local levy. Georgia has no statute on passing a repealed local tax to tenants.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Georgia follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (O.C.G.A. § 11-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (O.C.G.A. § 11-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. Georgia's contract law adds a rule of its own: accepting a check marked 'payment in full' for less than the total owed is an accord and satisfaction only if there is a genuine (bona fide) dispute about the amount due, or the payment is made under a separate agreement between you and the payer that it will satisfy the debt (O.C.G.A. § 13-4-103(b)). So if you have agreed to take a reduced amount, cashing the check settles the debt even without a dispute. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Georgia's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (O.C.G.A. Title 44, Chapter 7 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Georgia's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
